I once tried to make a cappuccino using the wrong machine, and it turned out more like a sludge. I nearly cried. Don’t even get me started. I once tried to use the coffee machine in the office and ended up burning my tongue. I told my boss it was a “flavor explosion,” and he just laughed. We should all just stop pretending we care about coffee. Let’s just take lunches together and stick to tea. It’s safer. I’m with you. I think the real issue here is that we’re all overthinking it. If we just ordered a tea, we’d be fine. Yeah, and if we can’t find good coffee, maybe we should just start a café ourselves. I’m in. It’s a business plan in the making. Or we could just go to the café across the street.

So, do you ever find it weird that social media is now like the main way people connect, even in libraries? I mean, I know we're all supposed to be about knowledge and information, but sometimes I feel like we're just posting about our coffee or our book recommendations instead of actually helping people. Yeah, I can't deny it. I mean, I use it for work all the time — like, tracking down resources, but then I also have my personal accounts. It’s funny how we’re all supposed to be in the information business, yet we're the first ones to be caught up in the scroll. Oh, I’ll tell you, it's the same in Australia. We have our own social media influencers, and they're all about bookstags and library challenges. I had one who followed me for a week and then just dropped me because I didn’t post enough about the Cats in the hat. I was like, “What?” That’s harsh. I’ve had that happen too, actually. I once posted a photo of a book I was reading with a caption like, “This book is taking me places,” and I got a message saying, “Seems like you’re not reading much.” I was like, “What? I read a whole book!” Oh no, that’s the same thing I got once. I was posting a photo of a library card and got a comment that said, “Try reading more, you’re not even on the list.” I just said, “Well, I’ve got my own list.” I think what it comes down to is that social media has this weird way of turning everything into a performance. You’re not just sharing about your interests — you’re trying to win the approval of an algorithm. It’s like a game where your likes are your score. Yeah, and we’re all in the business of ‘being seen.’ I mean, even in libraries, we’re starting to have open hours on Instagram, where people ask questions and we answer them live. I mean, it's a good way to engage, but sometimes I feel like we’re not really engaging with the people in front of us. Exactly. And sometimes, the people online are just not the same as the people in the room. I had a guy once who was ranting about libraries on Twitter, saying that they're out of date and not relevant.

So, do you think we've got enough information to move forward with the business case for the new hospice? I mean, the location is still a bit of a sticking point, isn't it? I think we need to do a bit more consultation with the local health services. We’ve talked about it, but we haven't actually spoken with the providers yet. They need to be on board if we're going to get the necessary funding. That’s true. And I’ve had some interesting discussions with the local council about the use of estate agents. Do you think we should go with a bidding process or just go straight to a local agency? I think a bidding process would give us more options and potentially a better price, especially if we’re looking to keep the budget tight. But I also understand that some of the local agents might have relationships with the hospices already. Exactly. We need to make sure this project is not just for us, but also considers the needs of the community, especially given the growing demand for end-of-life care. I’ve been thinking about the rationale for the location again—Tunbridge Wells has a decent population base, but is it close enough to the surrounding areas? It’s a good central point, but we might want to consider the proximity to existing hospices as well. If we’re going to compete for patients, we need to make sure they feel the services will be accessible. And we can’t ignore the nursing aspect. Our team will need to be well-trained in palliative care. Agreed. That’s why I’d like to bring in a specialist in end-of-life care to speak with the nursing team before we finalize the design. I think it would add value to the project. That sounds like a solid approach. Also, we need to think about the building itself. What do you imagine the new hospice will look like? Modern, open spaces? Or more traditional? I think a balance is key. We need to create a welcoming, peaceful environment that still reflects the professionalism of the service. I’d like to see more space for families, not just patients. That makes sense. The emotional support for families is crucial. And we can’t forget the politics of it all. The health budget is tight, so we have to justify every expense.

I can't believe we've got all these photos from when we first moved in. It's like looking back at a different life. Yeah, I remember when we first got the place. It was all bare walls and no proper kitchen. Look at this one—Lola was crying because she wanted a dog, and we couldn't have one. Oh, I remember that. You were so strict about the house rules. I think you even said something about not wanting a dog because of the mess. Oh, I did. I was scared of getting too attached. But look at us now, we’ve even got a cat. And it’s got the same name as my old cat. That’s sweet. I still remember the first time you brought her home. She was so shy, and I thought I’d never get her to come out of the box. I still have that photo on my phone. It’s one of my favorites. It’s like a snapshot of us, right before everything changed. Yeah, and I think that’s when you started working from home. You were always so stressed with your job, and this place gave you a bit of peace. It did. But I still have those old work emails from when I was preparing for Royal Ascot last year. I remember how stressed I was about it. You were so nervous about the interview. I still don’t understand why you didn’t just take someone else. You had so much experience. I know, I know. But I had this fear of not being able to do it. I still do, honestly. I’ve got a feeling I’m going to be applying for another job soon. You should. You’ve been working from home for too long. You need to get out there and do something more exciting. Maybe even apply for the Royal Ascot guest list? That would be amazing. You know, I was thinking about it the other day. I saw an ad for a copywriter position at one of those fashion brands. It’s a bit different, but it could be fun. Yeah, maybe you should try it. I’ve heard some of the people there are really cool. You could even use your skills for something like that. I’m sure you could. You’ve got that creative edge. But if you’re going to apply, you’ll need a new phone case.

So, do you watch horror films? I mean, I know you do, but I just want to know if you’re up for watching one tonight. I’m feeling like I need something scary to take my mind off this week. Oh, I’m always up for a good horror film. But seriously, have you seen  Hereditary ? I watched it last week, and I still haven’t stopped thinking about it. It’s like,  what the actual hell ? No, I haven’t. I’ve heard it’s really intense. I mean, I’ve watched  The Shining  like three times, and I’m still not ready to face the ghosts in that hotel. But I guess if you’re into it, I’m in. What are you in the mood for? I don’t know. I think I want something that’s not too graphic, but still gets under your skin. Maybe something with a slow build. Like  The Babadook ? It’s not as gory, but it’s really unsettling. Yeah, I’ve heard of that. I think it’s about a monster that lives in the mind, right? I mean, I thought it was more like a metaphor for grief. Doesn’t that make it even scarier? Because it’s not just something you can see—it’s something you can’t escape. Exactly! It’s that kind of horror that’s stuck with you long after the credits roll. I remember the part where the mom starts hallucinating and the babadook just stares at her. I had nightmares for a week after that. I’d be scared of that. I’m more of a  Saw  person. I like the whole setup of the traps and the moral dilemmas. But I guess I’m not as into the psychological stuff. Although I will admit,  Midsommar  is pretty good. It’s like a horror film but with a lot of bright colors and open spaces. It tricks you into thinking it’s not scary, and then you’re like,  what the hell was that?  Yeah, that’s the best part. It’s not just about being scared—it’s about being confused and unsettled. I think that’s the real horror. You don’t know what’s real anymore. True. I think that’s why I like watching horror with friends. You can laugh about it after, but while you’re watching, it feels like you’re actually in danger.

So, do you think I should get an iPad for the kids? I mean, they’re always on their phones, and I feel like an iPad might be more educational. Well, I suppose it depends on what you want it for. I had one when I was younger, but I found it just got in the way of my daily routine. I used to spend hours just scrolling through emails and not even doing anything useful. Yeah, I guess that’s a risk. But I think if it’s used properly, it could be a great tool. Especially with the kids wanting to learn more about tech. I mean, they’re already using apps and stuff. Maybe an iPad would help them get more organized? Organized? I think the only thing they’re organized about is their bedtime. They’ll be on their phones until the last minute, and then it’s a battle to get them into bed. Haha, I know. But I was thinking about getting an iPad for the youngest one. He’s got the attention span of a goldfish, and it might help him focus on something rather than just sitting there staring at the wall. Well, if you’re going to get one, maybe get a second-hand one from eBay? I saw one for sale the other day. It wasn’t new, but it worked fine. You can save some money that way. That could work. I’ll check the listings later. Oh, by the way, did you see the new Airbnb listing in Exeter? I was thinking about booking a weekend away with the family. It’s got a great review, and the host says it’s fully furnished. That sounds nice. I’ve always thought Airbnb was a great way to travel. You get a local experience, and you don’t have to worry about packing so much. Though I do miss the days when you’d just rent a room from a friend. Yeah, I know. But it’s easier now with all the apps and everything. You can just book it all in one place. True. I guess the world is changing. I remember when you had to call a hotel and wait on the phone for ages. No more of that. It’s amazing how technology has made things so much simpler. I mean, just the other day, I ordered a pizza online

So, do you remember that book we read last year,  The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle  by Haruki Murakami? I still can't get over how surreal some of the scenes were. Oh, I remember that one. That book had me completely wrapped up. But honestly, I think I read it more for the atmosphere than the plot. It felt like being in a dream, you know? Yeah, I get that. But it was also a great way to get out of my head and into something completely different. You know, sometimes when life gets too hectic, I need that kind of escape. Absolutely. And I think that’s why I’ve been trying to get back into reading more. I’ve been meaning to start a book club with some of the guys from the university, but I’ve been too busy with work. That sounds like a good idea. I’d love to be part of it. I’ve been meaning to read more too. Maybe we can even do some of the books we discussed in our college days—like  The Catcher in the Rye  or  The Great Gatsby . I love that idea. I think there’s something about reading those classics again that brings back all the memories. Though, honestly, I’m not sure I’d like  The Catcher in the Rye  as much now. You know what? I think you’d be surprised. There’s a lot of truth in Holden’s voice. And I read it a few years ago, and it made me think about my own teenage years. It’s strange how books can feel so personal after a while. Definitely. I think that’s why I’ve been getting into more travel writing lately. I’ve been reading books like  The Breadwinner  and  The Alchemist . They’re not the typical novels, but they transport you to places you’ve never been and make you think differently about life. That’s interesting. I’ve been meaning to read more travel stories too. I’ve been planning a trip to Japan for next year, and I wanted to get some books to read while I’m there. Maybe you could recommend something? That would be great. I’ve got a few recommendations. If you go to Kyoto, I think  The Tale of Genji  is a must-read. It’s one of the oldest novels in the world, and it really captures the essence of Japanese culture.

Mm, I just wanted to talk to you about the job application. I know it's been a bit of a process, and I’m not sure how I feel about it all. Of course, love. I’m here for you. What’s on your mind? I mean, I’ve been applying for a few positions, and I’ve had some rejections. It’s not that I’m not qualified—well, I think I am—but I keep getting told I need more experience. And I don’t have much. I know, sweetie. It’s tough, especially when you’re just starting out. But you’re so talented, and you’ve got that degree and the postgrad. You’ve got enough to stand out. I know, but it feels like no one is seeing that. I even applied for a few roles at firms I really admire, and I just got this generic rejection letter saying I’m not a good fit. That’s not fair. You’re not a bad fit. It’s just that the system is a bit… outdated, sometimes. I mean, don’t get me wrong, I’ve been in this industry for years, and I’ve seen how it works. I’m just worried about how long this is going to take. I’ve been working as a teaching assistant, but I want to do something more creative. I want to design spaces, bring ideas to life—this is what I dreamed about. And you are doing that, love. You’re working in a role that allows you to think creatively and be part of a team. Maybe that’s the stepping stone you need. I guess. But I still feel like I’m going in circles. Maybe I should look into doing some freelance work or even interning somewhere? That’s a good idea. You know, I did that when I first started. It’s a way to build your portfolio and gain experience without being tied down. And you’ve got the skills. You just need to put them to use. I keep thinking about what my dad said—about how he started in a similar place. He told me that the first job isn’t always the one that defines you. It’s about how you grow from it. Exactly. You’re not just learning how to design buildings, you’re learning how to navigate the world of work.

So, do you know, I was just thinking about how things have changed since I was a kid. Back in the day, you could walk to the shop and get your bread, and now you’ve got to wait in lines for cash points or whatever. It’s all so different. Yeah, it’s not just that, though. I think the whole system has shifted. You know, people don’t even know how to handle a bit of money anymore. I mean, I remember when you could get a job just for a few quid a day. Now, you’ve got to be a bloke with a degree to get anything. Aye, and the houses, too. I mean, I remember when the council houses were decent, you know. Now, it’s like you need to be rich to live in a house. I think the world’s gone mad with all the housing prices and the rents. I can’t even imagine paying that kind of money for a flat. That’s not just about money, though. It’s about the whole environment. I mean, I used to live in a nice little village, and now I can’t even find a decent spot to park my car without getting fined. You’ve got to be careful where you park, and then you got to pay for everything – even the road tax. I don’t know how they expect people to live like that. It’s all about government policy, really. You’ve got to look at the way they’ve gone about things. They’ve got to be trying to make it harder for people to get on the housing ladder, and it’s all because of the politicians who think they know better than everyone else. They make it so people are trapped in the system. I’m not saying it’s all bad, though. I mean, there are still some good things. The car, for example – the cars these days are better than they were back in my day. And the technology, too. I mean, you can surf the internet from your living room, and you can even order groceries without leaving the house. It’s all convenient. Yeah, but convenience comes at a cost. I mean, the more you rely on technology, the less you learn to do things the old-fashioned way. I remember when you had to wash your own clothes and cook your own meals.

I just got a call from the estate agent about the old warehouse space. They said there's been a lot of interest from local artists, especially from the ones who run the mural project in Vauxhall. It's quite a unique opportunity. That sounds promising. I was actually thinking about how we might want to use that space more effectively. It’s got good storage potential, and with all the creative types coming through, maybe we could host some pop-up exhibitions or workshops. Exactly. But there's something about the building that still feels a bit underused. I was walking past the fire escape the other day, and it reminded me of when we first moved in. It’s got character, but it also needs a bit of a facelift. Agreed. I was talking to the maintenance team yesterday about the storage areas in the basement. We’re thinking of moving some of the old furniture out and replacing it with more modern, functional pieces. It’d be great to make the space more welcoming for both tenants and visitors. That makes sense. I was also thinking about the marketing strategy—personally, I feel like we’re not really showcasing the building to its full potential. We’ve got such a diverse mix of tenants, from small businesses to community groups. Maybe we should highlight that diversity more in our promotional materials. That’s a good point. I’ve been looking into some new tools for tracking bookings and managing tenant relationships. It’s getting a bit overwhelming trying to keep track of everything manually. Maybe we could integrate a better system for managing holiday cover and staffing arrangements too. Definitely. I think the key is to maintain a good balance between the commercial side and the community aspect. We don’t want to lose our identity as a supportive, inclusive space. But at the same time, we need to generate enough income to keep things running smoothly. I couldn’t agree more. There’s also the matter of maintenance. The bird population in the building is getting a bit out of hand. I’ve seen a few pigeons nesting on the roof again. It’s a bit of a mess, but also a bit of a charm. Maybe we could put up some deterrents without making it too unpleasant for the tenants. That’s a good balance. I think we’re on the right track, but it’s going to take some coordinated effort between departments.

I can’t believe how good this roast is. I mean, I’ve had a few roasts in my time, but this one is just… exceptional. It’s got that perfect crust, and the inside is so tender. How do you even do that? Oh, it’s all in the preparation, mate. You’ve got to make sure the meat is seasoned properly, and then let it rest for a while before roasting. I borrowed the recipe from my aunt, who’s a bit of a culinary genius. She’s always been saying she’s going to write a cookbook one day. That’s not surprising. I mean, if you can cook a roast like that, you’d have to write a cookbook. My mum used to say that if you could cook a roast, you could cook anything. But honestly, I’ve never been able to get the hang of it. I tried once, and it turned out like a brick. Seriously, though, I think cooking is one of the things people take for granted. You know, when you’re not cooking, it’s like you’re not really living. I used to think that way when I was younger. Now that I’m older and more settled, I’ve started cooking more often. It’s a way to connect with people, you know? I agree. I think cooking is one of the best ways to bond with family. It’s not just about the food; it’s about the time you spend together. I remember when my parents were still together, we’d always cook together. Now, with everything going on, it’s hard to find the time. Yeah, I know what you mean. I’ve been trying to cook more, just for my flatmates. I’m not the best, but I’m trying. I’ve even started using cookbooks. I think it’s a good way to keep things interesting and not just rely on takeaway every day. That’s a great idea. I think I should try that too. I’ve been trying to cook more, but I always end up making the same things. Maybe I should start experimenting. I mean, who knows? Maybe I’ll become the next Michelin-starred chef. You’re not the first to say that. I go through phases like that too. One day I think I’m going to open a restaurant, the next day I just want to eat pizza and call it a day.

So, do you think we should go to Manchester for the weekend? I’ve been thinking about it since we were in Newcastle last month. Manchester? Why Manchester? You said you didn’t like the city. I didn’t like it back when I was like 16, but I think it’s different now. The city centre is really lively, and there's all that great music scene. Plus, I heard they’ve got some new restaurants opening up. You know, the kind of places that actually do good food. Yeah, I heard about the new place near Deansgate. It’s supposed to be amazing. But I still don’t like the crowds. I mean, it’s a big city, and I don’t know if I’m ready for that kind of chaos. I get that, but it’s not all chaos. Some parts are really nice. The area around the Castle is peaceful, and the museums are pretty cool. Oh, and I’ve got this plan to meet up with some old friends who live there. It would be nice to catch up. Old friends? You mean the ones from uni? Yeah, the ones from the engineering course. We didn’t really stay in touch, but they all got into good jobs. I think one of them’s even in London now. Anyway, it would be good to see them again. That’s a good point. I don’t get to see those guys much these days either. But I also don’t want to be stuck in a car for hours on the motorway just to get there. What about the journey? That’s true. The motorway can be a pain. But we could drive through York, right? It’s not too far and it’s a nice city to stop at. Plus, I heard there’s a new independent cinema there. I’ve been meaning to check it out. A cinema? You mean the one that shows indie films? That’s the one. I tried it once, and it was honestly one of the best experiences I’ve had in a while. The atmosphere is great, and the food is decent too. Yeah, I remember you saying that. I think the food is even better than some of the chain places. So maybe we can stop there for lunch? Then go to Manchester in the afternoon. Sounds like a plan.

So, do you know how it's going with your mum? I heard she had her operation last week. Yeah, it went okay, I think. She’s been in the hospital for a few days now. Not sure if they’re going to let her come home yet. That’s rough, I’m sorry. I didn’t know. You know, I’ve been meaning to call her, but I haven’t got around to it. It’s just… she’s been in and out of the hospital for months now. I don’t know how she’s holding up. It’s been really hard on the whole family. I can imagine. It’s always so hard when someone you love is unwell. I’m sorry you’re going through this. You must be really stressed. Yeah, you could say that. And it’s not just the hospital stuff. The funeral’s coming up, and we’re all trying to organise it. There’s been some arguments about where to hold it and who to invite. It’s not easy, is it? No, it’s not. I can’t even imagine how difficult it must be. I’ve been through a few funerals, but nothing like this. You’re so close to your family, aren’t you? Yeah, we are. But it’s not always easy. You know, even when things are hard, there are always opinions and disagreements. It’s just part of being a family. I guess that’s true. Some people just don’t know how to handle grief. I mean, I’ve seen some of my friends go through it and they just fall apart. I know. My sister had a really hard time after my dad passed. She started losing weight, and it was like she didn’t care about anything anymore. That’s awful. I think it’s important to take care of yourself during times like this. I mean, I’ve been trying to eat better lately. I know it’s not the same as being in a hospital, but it’s something. Yeah, I’ve been thinking about that too. I’ve been trying to eat more veggies and go for walks. It helps, a bit. But it’s not easy when you’re busy with everything else. You know what they say, you have to take care of yourself to take care of others.

So, do you two think you’ve got anything planned for the holidays? I know it’s still a bit early, but I’m trying to get my head around what’s going on with the kids. Well, I’m thinking about skiing, honestly. Dad said he’s got a few days off and he’s been talking about it for ages. But I’m not sure if I’m up for it. I’ve never done it before. Skiing? You’re not going to dump me in the snow, are you? I’ve got a car that’s still in the garage from last year. It’s been sitting there longer than I’ve been working. You’re not even going to be on the slopes, you’re just gonna be driving around pretending you know what you’re doing. Oh, come on, don’t be like that. You’re an operations manager, not a total layabout. You’ve got drive in you. Yeah, I’ve got drive in me, but not enough to go skiing in the middle of nowhere with no idea what I’m doing. But it’s not that far. It’s in the Lake District, isn’t it? It’s got mountains. Not all of them are covered in snow, though. And I’ve heard some of them are a bit of a climb. If you’re going, you’ll be the only one. Dad’s just going to be there with us. That’s the spirit. You’re not getting out of it. So, what’s the plan? Are you going to be in a group or just the three of you? I think the idea is we’re going with a few friends from school. They’ve got a few more people coming along. That’s good. Then you won’t be alone in the snow. Yeah, it’ll be fun. I mean, I haven’t done it before, but I’m not the only one. And if you’re not sure, you can always do something else. Some people go to the coast, or even around the UK. I’d rather do something adventurous than sit on a beach. I think I’d rather spend my holiday trying to keep up with a group of teenagers than just watching the sea. You’ve got to be joking. We’re 12. You can’t even drive without a learner’s permit.

So, do you remember that trip we took to Japan a few years back? I still have those old photos on my phone, but I’m thinking about getting them printed. I’ve been meaning to frame a few of them for the living room. Oh, I remember that! We were so lucky with the weather. I still can’t believe how clear the skies were in Kyoto. You know, I think I still have that photo of us standing in front of the Fushimi Inari shrine with all those red torii gates. It was such a magical moment. Yeah, that was one of my favorites. I still get a bit emotional every time I look at it. I’d love to print it out and put it on the wall. I’m thinking of starting a little photo gallery in the office. You know, to remind us of all the good times. That sounds like a great idea. I’d love to see that. I still have some of the photos from the trip too, but I never got around to organizing them properly. Maybe I should start going through them this weekend. You should. I’ve been thinking about doing the same. It’s funny how time flies, isn’t it? I mean, we were so young then, and now we’re already talking about our future plans. I can’t believe how fast it all happened. Yeah, it’s wild. I still have that little notebook I kept during the trip with all the notes and sketches. I think I still have the one I made of the cherry blossoms in Tokyo. It was so beautiful, and the way they bloomed in the spring—just magical. Oh, I still have that too. I even saved the screenshot of the map we used to plan our route. I remember we got lost a few times, but somehow we always found our way back. It was like an adventure every day. You were always the one with the map, weren’t you? I still laugh when I think about how you tried to read the Japanese street signs. We ended up getting a local to help us out, and it turned into one of those funny stories we still tell. Oh, remember when we got caught in that sudden rainstorm in Osaka? We were on our way to the temple, and we had to run for our lives.

So, did you go to Ireland last summer? Yeah, I did. It was like... shit, I thought I'd be able to relax, but I ended up getting lost in Dublin for three hours because I didn’t know where the pub was. Oh no, that’s not funny. I’ve been there, and I got lost too. My cousin said it was a test from the Irish gods. Yeah, I heard that. They don’t like tourists getting too comfortable. You know what’s even worse? Trying to find a decent meal. I mean, I couldn’t even find a place that wasn’t just a tourist trap. I know, I had this one meal where the lamb was so over-seasoned, I thought I was eating a dog. Wait, is that a real thing? No, that’s just me being a bit dramatic. But seriously, the food is amazing once you get to the right places. I thought the same, but then I ended up in this tiny place in Galway and the owner said, “It’s not the food, it’s the experience.” That’s a classic. I remember reading about that – it’s like, the vibe, the atmosphere, the whole thing. It’s not just Ireland, though. I’ve been to Australia and I’ve been told the same thing. You don’t just eat there, you experience it. Yeah, and I think that’s what it’s about. Like, being in a place and not just looking at it. You gotta live it. I guess. But still, I can’t help but think that if there was a zombie apocalypse, you’d be the first to be eaten. Oh come on, you’d be screaming like a little girl. No, you’d probably be the one trying to find a way to make a zombie apocalypse recipe out of whatever you could scavenge. Yeah, and I heard there’s a Jewish recipe for that. Claudia Roden wrote a whole book about it. Wait, really? Yeah, she’s like the queen of Jewish food. She’s got this amazing thing called “The Book of Jewish Food” which I think is like, seriously, the most impressive cookbook I’ve ever seen. I’ve heard of it. I think my uncle had it on his shelf. He swore by it. Yeah, he was like, “If you want to survive, you need to know how to make a good pastrami sandwich.”

So, do you ever think about how we're gonna get through this border thing? I mean, with all the security measures and everything, it’s like, you know, I can’t even remember the last time I went abroad without being questioned like a criminal. Honestly, I think it’s getting worse. I mean, I’ve got a friend who was at the airport last week and they had to take a full body scan just for carrying a small bag of peanuts. They said it was because of some new rule about food. You can’t even carry a bag of chips without it feeling like you’re trying to smuggle something. Yeah, I mean, peanuts are the worst, honestly. You know, like, what’s the problem with a bag of peanuts? I mean, they’re just nuts. I’ve got a bag of them in my bag right now. I’m actually planning to eat them while we watch this film. Oh, you’re going to watch a film? What film? The new James Bond one. I heard it’s got some crazy action scenes and a few computer games references. I think they even put in a scene where he’s playing a game. Kind of like, you know, a cross between a theme park and a computer game. Oh, really? I mean, I still think that the whole idea of theme parks and computer games being interconnected is a bit of a stretch. I mean, sure, they both involve some kind of virtual reality, but come on, a roller coaster isn’t exactly a game. Well, maybe not, but I think the filmmakers are trying to make it more immersive. I heard they spent millions on special effects, like, they even made a real-life version of the game’s main level. It’s like a theme park inside a movie. Wow, that sounds incredible. I mean, if they can do that, why not just make the movie a theme park? I could imagine a whole version where you ride through the movie with a headset and stuff. That would be cool, but I think it’s a bit too much. I mean, the whole point of the movie is to sit back and be entertained, not run around like a theme park. Although, I have to admit, I would love to see a real-life version of the game in a theme park.

So, how’s the rowing going? You mentioned you were going to start lessons last week. Oh, it’s going okay, honestly. I’ve got a few lessons under my belt now, and it’s actually quite fun. I never thought I’d be rowing on a river in Cambridge, but here I am, trying to balance the oars and not fall into the water. A lot of people find it tricky at first, especially if you’re used to being on land. I remember when I first tried kayaking, I just kept flipping over. Yeah, I can imagine. I mean, I’ve been kayaking once before, and that was on a very still lake. It was calm, but I still got nervous. I think the real challenge is the current, you know? Definitely. I suppose it’s about learning how to read the water, and how to adjust to the movement. You can’t just go with the flow, you have to fight it in a way. Exactly. It’s like learning to row, really. You have to work with the boat and the water, not against it. I think that’s what I’m starting to get. Speaking of water, have you thought about getting proper gear for wet weather? I mean, it’s been pretty rainy lately, and I’m sure you’d want to stay dry. Oh, I’ve actually been looking into that. I found this waterproof jacket online that’s supposed to be really good for kayaking. I’m hoping it’ll keep me dry in case I get caught in a sudden downpour. Sounds like a good idea. I remember the last time I went kayaking, I had this old raincoat that was barely holding together. I ended up soaked and cold. That sounds rough. I guess I should be more prepared. Speaking of preparing for things, have you heard the news about Auntie Margaret? No, what’s going on? She’s been in the hospital for a while with that illness she’s had. I think it’s something with her lungs. She’s not doing too well, and the family is really worried. Oh no, that’s terrible. I’m sorry to hear that. I hope she’s getting the best care possible. Yeah, it’s been tough. We’re all trying to make the best of it. It’s been a while since we saw her last, though.

Dad, do you know how to type in Morse code? I was trying to send a message to my friend on my phone, but I couldn't find the right app. Erm, I know what it is, but honestly, I haven’t used it since I was a kid. I think it’s more for radio operators and stuff like that. Yeah, I guess. But I saw a video online where someone used Morse code to send a text message. It was cool. It just used dots and dashes. You know, like the old telegraph stuff. Oh right, I remember that. My granddad used to send messages like that when he was in the navy. It was like a secret code, you know? He used to say it was the only way to communicate without being overheard. That’s so cool. I wonder if it’s still useful today. Wait, does it even work on phones? I think there are apps, but I don’t know if they’re reliable. Also, the way we text now, with emojis and shortcuts, you don’t need Morse code anymore. I mean, we’ve got emojis to show what we’re feeling, and everything’s just in text now. Yeah, but I think it’s kind of nostalgic. Like, it’s almost like a retro thing. I mean, the idea of sending messages without actually typing them out. It was cool to see that you could use just dots and dashes to make someone understand what you're saying. That’s true. I guess it’s kind of like the old days when people used to send letters through the post. It had a different feel to it. But I still think texting is way more efficient these days. I guess. But what if your phone dies and you can’t use it? Then you’d have to rely on something like Morse code to send messages. Although, I can’t imagine doing that on a phone without a special app. Exactly. I don’t think you can do it on a regular phone unless you’re using something like a Bluetooth device or a dedicated Morse code machine. It’s not something you can do just with your fingers on a touchscreen. I wonder if the schools teach that anymore. I mean, I don’t think they do in my college. I’ve never even had to learn it, but I feel like it would be useful for something like a competition or a special event.

Yo, man, it's been ages! You're looking good. How's life treating you? Bro, I’m good, thanks. It's been a while, man. How have you been? You still at university? Yeah, still rocking it. Just finished my final exams last week. Finally, I can say I'm done with that phase. That’s a relief. Man, I still have a few more semesters to go. I’m so over exams. Honestly, I just want to be done with them. Didn’t even want to sit for the last one. I know, man. I remember when I was in your shoes. You know, like that one time when I failed my mid-term and got so stressed I couldn’t even think straight. You were there, right? Oh man, you were the one who cried in the library. I remember that. I tried to comfort you, but I was just as stressed. We were both just faking it through. Yeah, like we were both trying to act like we were fine, but inside, we were crumbling. Remember when we tried to study together and ended up playing video games for hours instead? Oh man, that was epic. We ended up getting a bad grade, but we laughed about it for weeks. I’ve been looking up all this stuff—japanese food, temples, you know that whole vibe. That sounds awesome. I heard the food there is out of this world. I’m thinking of going to that ramen place on the internet. You know, the one that’s always on the list. Yeah, I’ve seen that. You should definitely check it out. Oh, and I heard there are these amazing tech cafes in Tokyo. You know, those places where you can work and eat good food at the same time. They’ve got like super-fast Wi-Fi and everything. Man, I need to go there. I’ve been thinking about getting a better laptop. My current one is starting to act up, and I’m tired of all the crashes.

So, do you remember that photo we took at Buckfast Abbey last week? It was the one where I was holding that big white cross and you were all like, “She’s going to fall over!” Oh, I remember that! I was laughing so hard, I nearly dropped my camera. I think that photo ended up on Facebook with the caption, “A pilgrimage to the spiritual home of the Black Death.” That’s a bit harsh, but I’ll admit, it did look like you were about to faint. Still, it’s a good story. Yeah, and then there was that moment when we got lost trying to find the abbey. I think we ended up in the middle of a sheep field, asking a farmer if he knew where the nearest church was. I still think he was trying to tell us we were already at the abbey. I remember that. You two were in a tangle of confusion, and I was just thinking to myself, “How did we get here?” It was hilarious. We were both so used to being in charge, and then we were just… wandering. Exactly. I mean, how hard can it be to find a religious site in Devon? I wouldn’t say it was hard, but I do remember you both getting quite frustrated when your phones started to die. Oh, right! We were out of signal for an hour. I was trying to send a message to my sister, and she was like, “Are you okay? You haven’t replied in hours.” You know, I was about to call the police. She said something like, “Don’t you dare.” That sounds like the kind of thing she would say. Anyway, we ended up finding the abbey, and it was beautiful. The monks were really friendly. They gave us some of their herbal tea, and it was amazing. I can’t wait to go back. Maybe next time we can take the whole family. That sounds like a good idea. Though I’m not sure if my wife would agree with me on a trip to a monastery. She’s more into the sea. She’d probably prefer a cruise. Exactly. I mean, if we’re going to travel, we might as well think about a cruise. I’ve been meaning to talk about that with you both. A cruise? You know I like that idea.

Mum, Dad, I am so glad you’re both back! How was Belgium? Did you enjoy it? Oh, it was absolutely beautiful, love. We had such a lovely time. The countryside was so peaceful, and the people were so friendly. Yeah, it was a real change of scenery. I’ve never been there before, but I reckon it’s got some of the most picturesque places I’ve ever seen. I heard you had some trouble with the sat-nav, Dad? Was that true? Oh, it was a mess. I think I got lost three times. I even tried to use Google Maps, but it kept giving me wrong directions. It was like a comedy of errors. I remember you saying you couldn’t find the way back to the hotel, and then you ended up in some random village with no Wi-Fi. It was quite an adventure, honestly. That sounds terrifying! I mean, what’s the point of a sat-nav if it’s not going to work? I had my phone with me the whole time, and I didn’t even use it because I thought it might be a waste of battery. I only used it when I absolutely had to. Yeah, and then there was the whole issue with the phone. I got a new one before we left, and I couldn’t even connect to the internet in Belgium. It was like trying to call home and getting no signal. Oh, that was the worst. I got so frustrated. I thought maybe it was just me, but then I asked the hotel staff, and they said the phone wasn’t compatible with the network over there. It was a real hassle. I can only imagine! But you did manage to get around eventually, didn’t you? I heard you went to the market in Bruges. Oh, we did. It was absolutely buzzing. All the stalls were full of fresh produce, cheese, and really good bread. The cheese was particularly amazing. I tried some goat cheese, and it was to die for. And the food! We had the best waffles and chocolate. I took some back with me for you, love. You’ll like them. Oh really? That’s so sweet of you. I can’t wait to try them. I’ve heard they’re the best in the world. They really are. And I must say, the locals were so kind.

I just thought I'd try making this risotto tonight, you know, something a bit different from the usual. I got the recipe from a blog—really simple, but I think it's going to turn out nicely. Sounds good. I like when things are a bit different. Although, honestly, I'm still not sure I trust myself with the stove. I think I burned the chicken last time I tried making something new. Oh, come on, you've made plenty of things. You just need to take it slow. I think the key is to not rush and just let things simmer. I like to think of it as a meditation. A meditation, huh? Well, I like that. I could definitely use some meditation. Though I’m not sure about the risks of using the stove as a meditation tool. I think I’d be more focused on avoiding the smoke alarm. Fair enough. But I think you’d be surprised how much you can do if you just take it one step at a time. And besides, the smell of the risotto—warm, creamy, and a bit nutty—it's really comforting. Yeah, I can imagine. Although, I still think there's something to be said for a good old-fashioned roast. You know, with the perfect roast potatoes and a bit of gravy. It just feels more... homey. I'll admit, I do miss the classics. But I also think there's something exciting about trying new things. Like, I recently picked up a perfume that's quite different from anything I've ever used before—light, fresh, and a bit floral. It’s like a new version of myself. Oh, I like that. I always thought perfume was a bit of an art form. I mean, not that I ever really thought about it before, but now that you mention it, I feel like I could use something a little more... confident. You could. You know, I was thinking about buying some flowers for the table too. You know, something with white and green—maybe some lilies or something like that. It’d add a nice touch to the meal. That sounds lovely. I think I’d like that. Though I still go back and forth about whether I should start a fire in the fireplace. I mean, it’s a bit of a hassle, but it does make the house feel cozy.

So, do you know much about Australia? Not really, to be honest. I’ve never been, and I don’t think I’ll go. I’ve got a few friends who say it's lovely, but I don’t think I have the kind of money to take a trip like that. Got a mortgage and a few other things to worry about. I’ve been there twice, actually. I taught English in Queensland for a few years. It was a bit of a culture shock at first, but I loved it. The people are so friendly, and the landscape is just amazing. You can’t really get that in England, can you? No, I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve been to the south of England a few times, and I know the weather’s never really good, but I’ve never been to Australia. I suppose I’d like to eventually, if I had the time and money. You know, I heard that people from the north of England, like me, have a bit of a reputation for being rough, but I don’t think that’s true. I mean, I’ve met people from all over the world, and they all have their own ways of talking. I sometimes think the Sheffield accent is a little too strong for some people to understand. Oh, I think it's a beautiful accent. It’s very distinct, and there’s a lot of character in the way people speak. I used to teach in Sheffield, and I got to hear all sorts of dialects. Some of the students thought I had a funny way of speaking, but I think it’s just the way people from Yorkshire speak. I suppose it’s about how you grew up. I was brought up in the south of England, so I never really got used to the northern way of speaking. I mean, it’s not that I don’t like it, but it just feels different. I can understand it, but sometimes it’s a bit hard to follow. Yeah, I hear you. I was brought up in Manchester, and even though I can speak standard English, sometimes when people from elsewhere come up to me, I have to do the whole Manchester thing for them to get it. That’s funny. I think it’s a sign of pride, really.

So, do you ever find it hard to stay off social media? I mean, I check my phone so much, even when I’m out with friends, I just find myself scrolling through something or another. It's like I can’t help myself. Honestly, I think I’m better than that. I try to limit my time on it, especially when I’m out with people. But sometimes, if I’m waiting for something, like for the food to come, I’ll just check my Instagram or TikTok. It’s like an automatic thing. Yeah, I get that. But I feel like I’m always missing out on real conversations because I’m too busy looking at videos or reading people’s posts. It’s like I’m not really present. Do you ever feel that way? Absolutely. I mean, I’ve been thinking about starting a podcast about teaching English as a foreign language. It’s something I really enjoy, and I’d like to get more people talking about the different methods and experiences we have. But I’m worried about how much time I’ll end up spending on social media trying to get it off the ground. That sounds amazing. I might have to listen to it. I’ve been thinking about starting a podcast too. I’m into all sorts of things—like history, food, and even some self-help stuff. But I’m not sure how to get started. Do you have any tips? Well, you could start by just recording yourself talking about something you’re passionate about. Even if it’s just a short episode, it’s a start. And don’t be afraid to post it online. People will listen if you have something to say. Plus, it’s a great way to stay connected with others who are interested in similar topics. That does sound doable. I guess I just need to take the first step. I’ve been thinking about it for a while, but I always put it off. Maybe I should start recording next week. It might be easier than I think. Yeah, I think you’ll surprise yourself. And who knows, maybe you could even start a podcast about veganism and teaching English—like how to incorporate ethical eating into language lessons. It could be really interesting. Haha, I didn’t think of that. But you know, I do love food, especially vegan food.

Alright, Pippy, you ready for today? Yes, I think I am! I brought my swimming goggles! I brought my floaties too! Excellent. Let’s get you both ready. I've been thinking a lot about this, honestly. I mean, I know it's a bit awkward, but... I don’t know how to bring it up. Yeah, I get it. I mean, it's not something you just casually talk about. But if you're feeling uncomfortable, maybe you should talk to someone about it. I know, but it's not just about that. I mean, I’ve been... I don’t know, feeling a bit disconnected from my body lately. Like, when I try to do things, it just... doesn't happen. That sounds really frustrating. Have you talked to a doctor about it? But it’s important to not let it fester. You don’t have to go through it alone. I know. I just... I don’t know where to start. What if it’s something serious? What if it’s... something I can’t fix? Yeah, but I don’t want to feel like a burden. Like, I don’t want to be the one who’s always asking for help. That’s not what it’s about. It’s about taking care of yourself. You’re not a burden. You’re just... human. And it’s okay to not have it all figured out right now. I guess. I just don’t want to feel like I’m missing out on anything. Like, relationships, intimacy... it all feels so far away. I know. But you don’t have to rush into anything. You can take your time. And if you need someone to talk to, I’m here. Thanks. I just... I don’t want to feel like I’m the only one going through this. You’re not. And that’s okay. You’re not alone. Yeah. I guess I need to start somewhere. And that’s the first step. Just talking about it. I guess. It’s a start. Yeah. And if you ever want to talk more, or need help finding a doctor, I’m here for you.

I was thinking about our holiday plans again. You know, we’ve been promising ourselves for months now that we’d go somewhere and actually relax, not just check off a list of tourist attractions. Yeah, I know. I’ve been meaning to ask you—do you still want to go to Portugal? I saw some pictures of the Algarve the other day and it looked absolutely beautiful. I do, actually. I just think we need to plan it properly this time. No last-minute flights or overpacked itineraries. Maybe take a couple of weeks and just be lazy. You know, read books, eat good food, and not worry about anything. That sounds ideal. But let’s be honest, I’d probably still be thinking about work. I mean, I’m not obsessed with it, but I do get a bit restless when I’m not challenged. I get that, but I think that’s just part of being in our line of work. You ever think about what you’d do if you weren’t working? Like, what’s your perfect day? Hmm, that’s a good question. Honestly, I think it’s something like this: waking up early, making a big breakfast, reading the paper over coffee, then going for a walk in the countryside. Maybe a picnic. Then, in the afternoon, just sitting in the garden with a book, maybe a glass of wine, and not worrying about anything. That’s kind of what I imagine. But I also think I’d like to have time to write. I’ve been thinking about starting a blog about my experiences as a PA. It’s been a while since I’ve had the time to put pen to paper. That’s a great idea. You have a really good way with words. I know that if you wrote a book, it’d be a bestseller. But, honestly, do you ever think about what you’d do if you were in a different line of work? Like, if you weren’t a PA? I do. I think I’d like to be a writer or a teacher. Something with more creative freedom. But I also know I’m not the kind of person who would survive in a job like that without a bit of structure. I get that. I think I’d be more like a gardener, actually. Someone who likes to be hands-on, and can take care of things.

Well, I think we've got the weekend sorted, but I do need to know if we're all in agreement about the weekend plans. Yeah, I think we are. I saw the postcard that Lucy sent from the Highlands, and I thought we should all take a trip up there for the weekend. That sounds good, but I was thinking of taking the kids up for a bit of a change of scenery. They've been stuck in the same house all week. Yeah, that's a good point. But I was also thinking of the birthday. You know, the one coming up in two weeks—Sarah’s. Should we start thinking about the party? Oh, definitely. I was just going to mention it. I think we should do something a bit different, maybe a small gathering at the house. It's been a while since we had a proper get-together. Yeah, I agree. But what’s the deal with the Scottish independence thing? I heard the news about the referendum, and I was wondering what you thought. Well, I think it’s a complicated issue. On one hand, I can see the arguments for independence—more control over local affairs, maybe a stronger sense of national identity. I’ll have to get in touch with the caterer and check if they’re free. Good idea. And if you need any help with the invitations, I can help with that. We could send them out over the next few days. That would be great. I’ve got the list of people who are coming, so I can make sure we have enough food and drinks. Perfect. And about the weekend trip—do you think we should go together or split up? Maybe we could split up. I can take the younger ones and you take the older ones.

So, do you think we should draw a chair for the Syrian refugees then? A chair? Like, a real chair? I mean, not a real chair, obviously. I just mean, we could draw a chair in the classroom to represent them. It’s a way to show we care, you know? But why a chair? Well, because when you’re in a refugee camp, you don’t have much. You don’t have a house, you don’t have food, you don’t have clothes. But you do have a chair. It’s a small thing, but it’s a symbol of dignity. Yeah, that makes sense. I mean, I guess it’s better than nothing. But what if they don’t even have chairs? That’s a good point. Maybe we should do a bit of research first. Maybe check some pictures or videos to see what kind of chairs they might have. Maybe we could draw different types of chairs? Like, a school chair, a wooden chair, a metal chair? That’s a great idea. It might help the kids understand the different kinds of chairs people have. And then we could talk about what kind of chair we have at home. Like, my chair is really soft and big. Yeah, and you can even sit on it for ages. But not all kids get that. It’s making me think about school, actually. Like, what if the Syrian kids come here and they don’t speak English? That’s true. We might need to help them with their schoolwork too. Maybe we can start a little tutoring group. Can I help? Of course, you can. Maybe you can help with simple math or spelling. What about tests? I don’t like tests. I always get nervous. I know, but tests are just a way to check how much you’ve learned. It doesn’t mean you’re bad at school. I don’t like tests either. I got a bad mark on my last one. Well, that just means you need to practice more. Maybe we can make it fun. Like, turn it into a game. Yeah, that could work. I mean, even if it’s just for the Syrian kids, it’s still important. Exactly. It’s about showing them that we’re here to help, and that school is a place where they can learn and grow.

So, do you remember that time we were on holiday in Cornwall and we got lost for hours? I think it was because of the signposts being upside down or something. Dad, do you remember when you first got a mobile phone? I think it was like the first Nokia ever. Oh yes, I remember that. I had a Nokia 3310, it was like a brick! But it lasted forever. I just got a call from the council. They’re talking about closing the local library. It’s really sad. I mean, it’s been there for decades, isn’t it? Yeah, I know. And they used to have those weekly book clubs and storytelling sessions. People used to come from miles around. It was more than just a library—it was a meeting place. And now they want to turn it into a parking lot? Or maybe a café? I can’t believe it. What’s the point of that? I think they’re trying to modernize the area, you know? But they can’t just knock down the building and replace it with something that doesn’t serve the same purpose. What about the people who rely on that library for free access to information and internet? That’s right. I mean, the internet is great, but not everyone has it at home. The library was a lifeline for a lot of people, especially the older ones. And what about the newspapers? I still go there to read the local paper and the old copies. It’s like looking back in time. Yeah, I can’t imagine what it would be like without them. I think the community should do something. Write to the council, maybe start a petition. People need to show they care. I agree. It’s sad to see things like that disappear. I was just looking at some old photos of the library online—there’s a whole history there. If they tear it down, they’ll lose that. I was thinking about the old upholstery fabrics too. I saw some beautiful ones at the market the other day. Those rich, deep colors. It’d be nice to have a place where people can sit and enjoy the space, not just be stuck in a café. That’s true. It’s not just about the books or the internet—it’s about the community.

So, do you know what’s the biggest stressor at work for me these days? It’s not the deadlines, or the emails, or even the meetings. It’s the constant need to check if I’m being recorded. I swear, every time I answer a question, I half expect someone to be listening in. That’s crazy. It’s not that funny. I think it’s one of those things that just gets passed around like it’s some kind of inside joke. So, do you think we should go vegetarian? I mean, I’ve been thinking about it more since I started reading about the environmental impact of meat production. It’s a bit futuristic, but I think it could go a long way in reducing animal cruelty. I agree. It’s kind of like the dream of the future, right?

So, do you know what’s happening with the Alumni Day tomorrow? I was just thinking about it, like, I haven’t seen you in ages. I’m so glad we’re both here today. Yeah, I know, it’s been a while!
