You could get scammed, or even worse, someone could find out your real identity and mess with you. I don’t know why people even do it. I think it’s just the internet, you know? It’s like a big playground where people think they can be anyone they want. But the problem is, when it comes to real life, they’re still real people with real feelings. That’s true. I remember reading about a guy who fell for someone he met online, and when he found out it was a guy pretending to be a woman, he was completely devastated. It’s like, you invest so much time and emotion, and then it’s all a lie. Ugh, I can’t even imagine going through something like that. I mean, I’ve been on dating apps, but I just stick to the basics. You know, what’s your name, what do you do, what are you looking for? Yeah, I think that’s safer. I mean, even Jeremy Kyle talks about how people are more honest now because they know they’re being watched. It’s like, they can’t just play games anymore.

So, do you remember the time we went to Paris together? I think it was around the time I was first studying Classics, and I was absolutely obsessed with French literature. I think I even tried to read  À la recherche du temps perdu  in the middle of a café in Montmartre. Oh yes, I remember that. You were so determined to prove you could read in French, even though you hadn’t actually studied it properly. I think you got lost on the Rue des Études for like half an hour trying to find the bookshop. Didn’t even speak a word of French. I know! I was so proud of myself, thinking I was such a culture vulture. But you know, I still haven’t finished that book. I’ve tried a few times, but I always get distracted by the internet or something. Sometimes I just watch videos of bees instead. Bees? You’ve been watching bee videos again? I thought you said you were going to stop that after the last time you got so absorbed in it that you forgot your own name. Yeah, I was in the middle of a lecture, and I just… zoned out. I think I still might have been on a bee hive documentary. I remember the professor got so frustrated. He said, “Mr. Thompson, are you even paying attention?” and I just said, “I am! I’m just thinking about the waggle dance!” Oh, you’re such a weirdo. But I also think you’re a bit of a genius. I mean, you translated that whole German poem about bees in your first year at university. That was impressive. Yeah, I did. I think it was the only time I ever really got a mark above 70%. Everyone else thought it was nonsense, but I was convinced it was a classic. I still do. I mean, the language is beautiful, even if the grammar is a bit confusing at times. You know, I once had a professor who spoke German and he said your translation was one of the best he’d seen from a student. He even sent it to a friend in Austria. I think the friend was from Vienna, like me. You know, I sometimes think about going back there. I mean, I’ve been there a few times, but I always feel like I’m not quite living in the same city as the people who grew up there.

So, do you think we should be going faster? I mean, we’re already an hour late, and we’ve got another hour to go. Oh, don’t be so dramatic. It’s only a 2-hour drive. We’ve got time. And it’s not like we’re stuck in traffic. I mean, the roads are clear, and the weather’s actually nice for a change. A bit too warm, but that’s fine. Yeah, but I still think it’s a bit risky. I heard about this new stretch of road near Weymouth that’s supposed to be really dangerous. I mean, I don’t want to end up in the ditch or something. Oh, don’t be so paranoid. I’ve driven that route a hundred times, and I’ve never had any issues. Besides, the Sat Nav said it was the fastest way. Maybe it’s just the Sat Nav. I’ve had friends who followed it and ended up in the wrong town. You know, the kind that’s like, ‘Oh, this is the way, but it’s actually a place called ‘Boringborough’ or something like that. And then they had to turn around. That’s not funny. I mean, I’ve heard stories about people getting lost in Dorset, and some of them ended up in the countryside and couldn’t find their way back. It’s not even that far, but you can be stuck for hours. Oh, come on. We’re not that far off. Plus, I’ve got the phone with the maps app. If we get lost, we can just check it again. Yeah, I guess. But what if the phone dies? You know, like last time when I was on my way to pick up my mum from the hospital and it just shut down. I had to ask a stranger for directions, and he was like, ‘Oh, you’re going the wrong way. Turn around!’ So I did, and then I ended up at a theme park instead of the hospital. That’s not funny. I mean, I’m a student, and I’ve got exams coming up. I just don’t want to be stuck in some place with no signal or bad coverage. It’s not like I can just stop and ask for directions like you can. Yeah, I know. You’re always worrying about technology.

I've been thinking a lot lately, you know. Oh, what about? Just about things... Life, you know. I mean, I've been retired for years, and it's funny how time just flies. One day you're working like mad, and the next, you're just sitting here with a cup of tea and a newspaper. I know what you mean. I feel the same way. I used to be so busy with the kids, and now it's just me and the cat. Yeah, the cat's a good listener, isn’t she? She’s got her moments, I'll give her that. But sometimes I think she’s just waiting for me to die. Oh, don’t say that. You’ve got a good life. You’ve got the house, the garden, and a nice quiet place to be. I suppose. But I do miss the kids sometimes, you know? I know. I miss them too. They grew up so fast. One day they were running around the garden, and now they’re off to university and all that. It’s strange. You think you've got all the time in the world, and before you know it, they’re all gone. Yeah. But I suppose that’s the way of things. You can’t stop time. No, you can’t. But maybe we can make the most of what we’ve got. Exactly. I think I’ve been feeling a bit lost lately, you know? Like, what’s the point of all this? I hear you. But I think it’s about enjoying the little things. Like the sunrise, the tea, the quiet moments. That’s true. I guess I just need to remind myself that I’m not alone. I’ve got you, and I’ve got the cat, and I’ve got this house. And we’ve got each other. That’s what matters, isn’t it? Yeah. I think I’ll try to focus on that. Good. And if you ever feel like you're losing your way, just come and see me. I'll always be here. You know I will. Thank you, love. Anytime. And don’t forget, life’s still worth living. Yeah, I know. It’s just... I need to remember that. We all do. That's what friends are for. Yeah. So, let’s just sit here and enjoy the silence, huh?

So, do you know what’s been playing on repeat in my head all day? That new album by The National. It’s got this really jangly guitar sound and these lyrics that just… stick with you. It’s like they’re telling a story, but in a really cryptic way. I’ve heard a few tracks, but I haven’t really got into it yet. I’m more of a fan of the more melodic stuff, you know? I mean, I like The National, but I think I prefer bands like The Strokes or Arctic Monkeys for the vibe. Maybe it’s just because I like the more upbeat sound. I get that. I think The National is more about atmosphere and mood, though. Like, you can almost visualize the scenes they’re describing. I was thinking about the song “Fake Empire” the other day—it’s got this kind of storytelling that feels like it’s coming from somewhere real, like a real memory or a real place. That’s interesting. I guess I’m more into the emotional immediacy of music. It’s easier for me to connect with songs that feel raw or personal. I mean, I’ve been listening to a few of my old favorites lately, like Radiohead—especially  OK Computer . It feels like it was made during a time of huge change, and I can still feel that tension in the music. Yeah, that’s a great point. I think that’s why music can be such a powerful form of communication. It doesn’t always have to be literal. Sometimes it’s just about evoking a feeling or a moment. Totally. It’s funny, because I’ve been talking to a few of my friends about how we’re all feeling the same way about the weather lately. It’s been so unpredictable. One day it’s sunny and warm, and the next it’s raining cats and dogs. I swear, it’s like the sky’s got a mind of its own. I know, right? I was out gardening the other day, and I was waiting for the sun to come out so I could get some of the plants watered. And then—  boom —it starts raining. I almost had to run back in with a bucket and a towel. It was ridiculous. I had that happen too. I was trying to get some fresh air and enjoy the weekend, and then I got caught in what felt like a storm straight out of a James Bond movie.

So, do you know, I’ve been thinking a lot about unemployment lately. It’s like, it’s everywhere, isn’t it? I mean, I’m in a higher professional occupation, but I still feel this weird pressure that if I’m not working, I’m failing somehow. Yeah, I get that. I mean, even though I’m a PhD student, I still get that same nagging thought that I should be working full-time. It’s like, what if I don’t get a job after this? What if I’m just… stuck? Exactly. And it’s not like we’re in a position where we can afford to be unemployed for long, you know? I mean, my parents are still around, but I’m not sure how long that will last. And I know you’ve been trying to get a job for months now. Yeah, it’s been a struggle. I’ve had a few interviews, but nothing’s really stuck. I keep thinking, “Okay, this one’s going to be the one,” but then it just… fizzles out. I know the feeling. It’s like you’re constantly putting yourself out there, but no one’s taking the bait. And then there’s this guilt, like, “What if I’m not good enough?” It’s so frustrating. I mean, I’m in a postgrad program, I’ve got the qualifications, and yet I’m still struggling to find work. It’s like the system isn’t working for people like us. I think you’re right. I mean, I worked in a research role for a while, and it was good, but I wanted more. I wanted to be doing something creative, or something that made an impact. But now, I feel like I’m just… waiting. Maybe that’s the problem, though. When you’re in education, you’re used to working on projects, not on a day-to-day salary. It’s like, you start to lose the ability to just… stick with one thing for long. Except, with university fees, you can’t just do that. I mean, I paid a lot for my postgrad course, and now I’m in a position where I’m not even working full-time. It feels like I’m paying for something that I’m not even getting a return on. I know. I mean, I’ve had to take on some part-time jobs, like tutoring or helping out with research, but it’s not enough.

So, do you think we should include some of the family stories in the book? I mean, it would be nice to have something that the kids can read and learn about us. That sounds like a great idea. I think it would help them understand where they come from. But maybe we should start with the basics—like the family tree first. It’ll make things easier for them to follow. A family tree? Oh, that’s a lovely thought. I remember when I was teaching, I used to have my students draw family trees for their history projects. It’s a great way to show connections. But I think including some of the stories would make it more personal and meaningful. Yeah, I agree. I was thinking about including some of the stories about my dad, like how he used to tell us about his brother who moved to Australia. It was always funny, but also gave us a sense of where we came from. That sounds like a good start. I was actually thinking about including the story about my stepdad. He was such a character—always telling jokes, even when we were in a bad mood. I think the kids would love to read about that. Oh, I’d love to hear that. I remember when I was young, my mother used to tell me about her own parents and how they met. It always made me feel connected to my roots, even if I couldn’t remember them myself. That’s true. Our family has such a rich history, even if some of it is a bit scattered. I think the book could help bring it all together. What do you think, Mum? I think it would be a wonderful way to pass down the stories. I just hope the kids take an interest. I know they’re pretty busy with their own lives right now. Well, that’s the beauty of it. You never know when a child will want to know more. I have a grandchild who always asks me stories about my childhood. I think it’s important to keep those traditions alive. Yeah, I’ve been thinking about that too. Maybe we can include some pictures as well? It would make the book more engaging for the kids. That’s a good idea. I can help you find some old photos. I have a box of them in the attic.

So, do you ever just get fed up with shaving? I mean, it's like, every morning, you're like, “Oh god, I have to do this again.” Yeah, honestly, I do. I mean, it's not even that I don't like it — it's just the whole process. Like, the razor, the cream, the irritation, the fact that you're basically making yourself bleed a little every time. I know, right? It's like you're not just shaving — you're doing a full ritual. And yet, if you don't do it, you're like, “Oh no, I look like a weirdo.” Exactly. My mum always said, “If you don’t want to look like a ginger, you better shave.” But honestly, I’ve been thinking about just letting it grow in for a while. Oh yeah? What’s the plan? Are you going to start with just a little bit, or are you going full beard? I don’t know. I mean, I’ve got some facial hair, but I don’t really like it. It’s like, I can’t even tell if it’s growing in properly or if I’m just making it worse. I get that. I’ve tried growing it out once, and it just looked like a weird bush. And then I couldn’t even go out in public without feeling like I was dressed as a pirate. Oh no, that’s a nightmare. I can’t imagine that. But I’d rather have a little stubble and be comfortable than feel like I’m cheating on my skin. I think I’m starting to feel the same way. I mean, I like having some sort of texture, but I don’t want to look like a grizzled man. Maybe I’ll just do the whole “clean-shaven” thing for a week and see how I feel. Sounds like a plan. Although, I’m still convinced that if you don’t shave, you’ll end up with a full beard by the end of the month. Yeah, that’s what I’m worried about. But maybe I’ll just go for the buzzcut. You know, like a buzzed head, but with some stubble. It’s like a compromise. Okay, but you’ll have to let me know how it goes. I mean, if you’re going to start experimenting, I want to be the first to know.

So, do you know what’s the biggest thing about the alphabet? I was trying to think of a way to remember it and I thought, maybe if I associate each letter with something from my life. Like A for “Alcohol,” because we were talking about that earlier— Yeah, we were. And I thought, maybe we shouldn’t be talking about alcohol if we’re not actually drinking. But I reckon we’re gonna have a few pints anyway. Yeah, I know, but it’s just me thinking out loud. So, A for alcohol, B for… boxing? Because I went to a fight last week. Boxing? You? That’s a bold move. You’re not the type to get into a fight. I didn’t get into a fight, I just watched one. A heavyweight fight at the pub. It was amazing. You need to get out more. I mean, if you’re going to be in a pub, you might as well get a drink. I did. I had a pint, and then I thought about how much I miss the days when I didn’t think about alcohol at all. That’s a funny thing to say. You’re a research manager, for God’s sake. You’re not even supposed to be thinking about alcohol. Well, maybe I’m just getting older. I don’t know. Anyway, moving on. So, C for… race. Oh, you’re bringing up racism in football now? Yeah. I saw a documentary the other day about it, and it made me think. I mean, I’ve never seen it firsthand, but I know it’s a real issue. I know. I grew up in Birmingham, so I’ve seen it. You can’t just ignore it. It’s like, you can’t just say, “Well, it’s not my problem.” I know. I think it’s about awareness. Like, if you’re not aware of it, you can’t fix it. Exactly. And that’s what I’m trying to do with my PhD—look at the systemic issues in football. That’s cool. I respect that. It’s not just about the players, it’s about the culture, the fans, the media. The whole thing. Yeah. And I think people like you, who are into research and analysis, are the ones who can actually make a difference. I hope so. I mean, I still drink, so I can’t say I’m completely out of the picture.

I just got a call from the council about the request for funding for that old mill in Radley. They’re considering it, but they want more specifics on how the renovation would preserve its historical value without overburdening the budget. I can see that. They’re always cautious with heritage projects. You know, they’ve got to balance the need to keep things authentic with the practicalities of making a building habitable these days. Exactly. And I think they’re concerned about the structural issues. We’ve had a few emails from them asking for more details on the engineering assessments. I’ve been meaning to get back to them with a more comprehensive report. You should. And maybe think about how you can present the project in a way that shows it’s not just about preservation, but also about creating a sustainable space. They might be more inclined to fund it if they see it as a viable long-term investment. That’s a good point. I’ve been thinking about how to frame the proposal. Also, the local history society has been quite supportive. They’ve offered to help with some of the documentation. Maybe we can include their input to strengthen the case. Definitely. They have a lot of local knowledge and can add weight to the historical significance. But we need to be careful not to overstate things. There’s a fine line between passion and exaggeration when it comes to heritage projects. Absolutely. I remember when I was working on the old village hall in Wotton. We had to be very precise with the evidence we presented. Also, it’s important to think about community engagement. If the locals feel invested in the project, it can make a big difference. That’s true. I had a client a few years back who wanted to convert an old bakery into a boutique hotel. At first, it seemed like a risky move, but once we got the community on board, it worked out. The key was showing how the project would benefit the area as a whole. I like that approach. It’s not just about the building itself, but the people who use it and the place it’s in. Speaking of which, have you heard anything about the funding application deadline for the next round? Not yet, but I’ll check with the office.

So, do you know what’s really interesting about the way people speak in different parts of England? I was reading this article the other day about dialects and how they’re changing, especially with the rise of digital communication and social media. It’s like we’re all kind of blending our accents now. I saw that too. I think it’s because people are exposed to so many different accents through TV, radio, and online platforms. Like, I used to be pretty conscious of my Birmingham accent, but now I don’t even notice it as much. It’s like the whole country’s becoming more of a hybrid. Yeah, I mean, I still notice the differences when I go back to Sunderland. You can tell the local people from the ones who’ve moved up here for university or work. It’s like their accents are starting to shift too. Do you think that’s a good thing or a bad thing? I think it’s natural. Languages and dialects evolve all the time. But I also worry that some of the older, more distinct regional accents are getting lost. I mean, I grew up hearing the Midlands accent, and it’s pretty different from what I hear now. It’s like the way people speak is changing in real-time. That’s true. I’ve been thinking about how my own accent has changed since I moved to Cambridge. I used to speak a lot more like someone from the north, with that ‘r’ sound and everything, but now I’ve kind of adopted a more standard English accent. It’s not like I’m trying to sound posh or anything—just that the environment here influences how you speak. I can definitely relate. I’ve been trying to do some research on accent acquisition and how it’s affected by different social groups. I think it’s more about the social context than anything else. People tend to mimic the way people around them speak, especially in academic or professional environments. That makes sense. I was actually talking to my mum about it the other day. She’s from Sunderland too, and she said she’s noticed that even her own accent has gotten softer over the years. She says it’s because of the way younger generations speak now. It’s like we’re all becoming more like each other, even if we go back to our hometowns.

So, do you remember what we were talking about earlier? About the school dinners and eating at Granny’s? Yeah, I remember. I think I said I like eating at Granny’s better than school dinners. That’s true, isn’t it? Granny’s meals are always so much better. But I guess the school has to provide something for everyone. I don’t like school dinners. They’re always too salty. Yeah, I know what you mean. My brother was always complaining about the fish and chips they serve. But he’s not supposed to eat that, you know. Wait, why not? Because it’s not healthy. And he’s on a budget, so we can’t just buy him fancy food all the time. But isn’t there a school dinner fund? I think I heard something about that. Yeah, there is. It’s called the “school meal money.” You have to pay a small fee for each meal, so that the school can afford to provide food. So, if you don’t pay, you can’t eat at school? Exactly. But it’s not just about money. Some kids – like my brother – can’t afford it, so they skip meals. That’s why we need to make sure he has enough money for the meals. What about the tennis tournament? Is that going to cost money too? Oh, that’s a good point. The school is organizing a tennis tournament, and it’s going to cost a bit to enter. Some of the kids have to pay to participate. That’s not fair. Not everyone can afford that. I know. But it’s a competition, and they have to raise some funds. Maybe we can help out if needed. What if the school can’t afford to pay for the tournament? Then they might not be able to do it. That’s exactly what we’re trying to avoid. We need to make sure the school has the money to run things properly. I wonder if the school has any other events that cost money. Like the circus or something? Oh, you’re thinking of the school fair. They had a clown and a magician last year. The kids all loved it. But it did cost quite a bit to set up. I think the school used some of the funds from the previous events. Like the food sales and the raffle.

So, did you enjoy the film we went to see last night? I thought it was pretty good, but I know some people didn’t like it. I did, actually. I found it a bit thought-provoking. It made me think about how history is taught now versus how it was when I was at school. I remember the history lessons being pretty dry, just dates and facts. Now, I hear that there's a lot more discussion around how to present it, especially with the current national curriculum. Yeah, I’ve heard about that debate in Cambridge. It’s interesting. Some people argue that history should be more about understanding different perspectives, while others think it’s too political. Honestly, I think there’s a balance needed. You can’t just have students memorizing dates; they need to understand the context and the causes and consequences of events. I agree. My students sometimes complain about how much they have to memorize, but I always tell them that understanding the big picture helps them connect the dots. It’s kind of the same with Higher Education, isn’t it? I mean, you need both theory and practical experience. I think that’s what the debate is about—how to integrate real-world applications into the education system. Absolutely. When I was in school, I remember doing a project on the Industrial Revolution and actually visiting a local museum. It made a big difference. But these days, with the national curriculum, it seems like there’s more focus on exams than on real-life relevance. I wonder how that affects students’ long-term understanding. That’s a fair point. I think the key is to make sure that education isn’t just about passing exams but about developing critical thinking and analytical skills. I’ve always believed that industry experience is valuable, especially when it comes to Higher Education. Going into the advertising world, I had to constantly adapt and think quickly—skills that are definitely transferable to any academic or professional setting. I couldn’t agree more. It’s not just about what you learn in the classroom; it’s about how you apply that knowledge in the real world. I’ve seen students who are brilliant in theory but struggle when it comes to practical applications. That’s where experience really helps. Exactly. That’s one of the reasons I think it’s important to talk about how to organise Higher Education degrees in a way that bridges the gap between theory and practice.

I've been thinking a lot lately about the war, you know. Not the one in Ukraine, but the first one, the one that changed everything for us. Oh, yes, that's right. I remember when we were kids, the air raids were a big deal. My mum used to make sure we had our blackout curtains pulled down every night. It was a different time altogether. I was too young to remember much, but I’ve heard stories from my father about how people used to keep food hidden in the garden. You never knew when the bombs would drop. It's amazing how the war shaped so much of our national identity. Even now, people still talk about that era like it was just yesterday. Yeah, and I think it's partly because we lost so much. The whole world seemed to be at war, and we were just trying to get through each day. I remember my brother being drafted into the army at nineteen, and it broke my mother's heart. That must have been terrible. I can't imagine losing anyone so young. I still get emotional when I think about the children who were sent off to fight in the war. It's interesting how time passes, isn't it? I remember my father talking about how he was in the army, and how he used to come home with stories of the front line. He always said the war taught him resilience. I suppose that's true in a way. But I wonder how people today feel about war. I mean, with all the technology and the way the world is now, do they still see it as something people are forced into? I think the younger generation doesn’t really understand what it was like. They’ve never lived through anything like that. I tell my grandsons stories about the war, and they just laugh. They’re young, I know. But I worry they'll grow up without understanding the sacrifices that were made. I always tell them to appreciate what they have. I agree. But then again, we've had our share of conflicts over the years. Some people still talk about how the country was run during the war, the rationing, the long queues for bread and butter. It was a real test of how people got on with each other.

So, do you think we’ll be able to fit all our stuff in the car? I mean, it’s not like we’re moving to another country or anything, but I still feel like we’ve got a lot to carry. No, I think we’ll be fine. We’ve got the van and the car. I’ve already packed the bigger items in the van. You just need to make sure you clean out the fridge and the cupboards in the flat before we leave. If we leave it all in, it’s just going to be a mess for whoever takes over. Yeah, I know. It’s just weird, you know? I mean, we’ve lived there for six years, and now it’s our last night. I feel like I should be sad, but honestly, I’m just tired. Every time I think I’m ready to leave, something else comes up. I get it. I’ve been thinking about it too. I remember when we first moved in, it was so exciting, right? I mean, we thought we were starting a new chapter of our lives. Yeah, and we did. But now, it’s like, time to move on. I still can’t believe we’re actually going to be moving in with the in-laws. I mean, it’s not like I didn’t think it would happen eventually, but the timing is just… odd. You know what? I think it’s more about the fact that you’ve been working full-time for so long. You’ve been a teacher, and I’ve been working in customer service—there’s just not much time for being a family. I mean, we’ve been there for most of the kids’ lives, but the days just kept going, and before we knew it, it was time to make a change. I guess. And besides, I still have that mortgage to pay off. I mean, even if we’re not moving for the best reasons, the financial side of it was always a big part of the equation. Yeah, and you did well. I mean, you’re young, you’ve got your teaching job, and you’ve got the extra courses. You’re set for the future. That’s what I keep telling myself. But I still miss the flat. I miss the kitchen, the way the light came through the window, and the fact that I had my own space.

Right, so I just got the list of people coming for the birthday. Let me just check it again. Okay, got the names, and I’ve got the seating plan I was going to do. But I think we need to make some changes. Yeah, I agree. We haven’t included Auntie Mabel yet, and we’ve got the cousin who’s got a baby now—should we make a table for them? Also, I think the table near the window is going to be too small for the extended family. We might need to move the seating around. Definitely. And don’t forget the three from the old school friends group—Tom, Lucy, and Dan. They’re bringing their kids too. My mum said she’d like to sit with the relatives, not the friends, so I’ll need to adjust that. Right, and then there’s the question of the menu. I know you wanted to do something special for your mum’s birthday—maybe a bit of a themed menu? Maybe something with the Great British Bake Off? I saw one of those themed dinners on the internet. That sounds good. I mean, we did a similar thing last time and everyone loved it. But we’ve got to be careful with the dietary requirements. Julie from the church is vegetarian, and Richard is allergic to nuts. Also, there’s the other cousin who’s into raw food. It might be complicated. I know, but we can keep the main dish as a classic roast with sides and then have a few options. Maybe a vegetable quiche, a meat pie, and something for the raw food crowd. I can check with the caterer about the options. Perfect. And I think we should add some candles to the table. We’ve had the candles from the last party, but maybe we can put some new ones on the cake as well. The old ones are starting to look a bit worn out. Yeah, and I remember you said you wanted a table plan with photos of the family. I can print out some pictures of the kids from the past and put them on the sides. It’ll make it more personal and nostalgic. That’s a great idea. Also, I’ve been thinking about the fish we’re buying. I need to check if the fishmonger still has the fresh cod and haddock.

So, do you remember when we were in the clinic and they said I needed to get my wisdom teeth out? I was so scared, honestly. I mean, I thought I’d be fine, but when they told me it was going to be a three-hour operation, I just started panicking. I remember that! You were so stressed, you couldn’t even sit still. I think you even tried to run away when they were about to put the anaesthetic on. Yeah, I know. I was just so worried about the pain and the recovery. But, honestly, it wasn’t as bad as I thought. Still, I’ve got these massive holes in my mouth now, and it’s like they’re just waiting for something to fall in. I feel you. My mum always says I should have listened to her and gone to the dentist more often. She’s always been telling me about how important it is to take care of your teeth, but I just rolled my eyes every time. Now I’ve got to deal with the consequences. I know, I know. My parents are always asking me when I’m going back to uni. They’re like, “Oh, you’ve got to get a flat, you’ve got to start saving money, you’ve got to get a job.” It’s like they think I’m suddenly going to be an adult. I’m still living in a student flat, for goodness’ sake! I get that, but I think they just want to make sure you’re settling in. I mean, I’m going back next term, and my parents are already talking about moving house. They want to get something bigger, closer to the city because they say it’s easier to walk to the station. Oh, I’m so jealous. My flat’s got a hole in the ceiling, and it’s a nightmare to cook in. My roommate’s always leaving the fridge open, and I can’t even trust the oven to work properly. I think I’m going to move out soon. You should. Honestly, I think you’d be better off on your own. Just make sure you don’t end up with a hole in your ceiling like mine. I’m still trying to fix it, and the plaster is still goopy. I don’t think I can handle another hole.

Alright, so I was thinking about doing something kind for the community this year. You know, like that thing where you do a random act of kindness every day? Yeah, I heard about that! It’s supposed to be really nice, right? Like, you just do something small but meaningful for someone else. I think it’s like, you don’t have to do anything big, just something that makes someone feel good. Exactly! So, maybe we can start by helping someone in need. You know, like the lady at the shop who always smiles at us. Maybe we could leave her a note or something. That sounds good. Or maybe help out with the local food bank? I’ve heard they’re always in need of volunteers. I like that idea. But I’m not sure if I’m up for volunteering. What if I’m too shy? You don’t have to volunteer for long. Maybe just help out for an hour or two, and then you can say you did it. It’s a good way to get out of the house too! I think that’s a good plan. But what if we do something for Chinese New Year? I mean, it’s coming up soon, and we’re all British, but I know a lot of people in the area celebrate it. Yeah, I think my mum’s Chinese and she’s always talking about how people celebrate with lanterns, food, and family. Maybe we could help out with something like that? That’s a great idea! We could set up a little event in the community garden. Like a mini festival with Chinese food, decorations, and maybe even some games. It would be a way to bring different cultures together. I love that! We could also make some lactose-free cakes and cookies for the event. My sister is allergic to dairy, so I’ve been practicing making lactose-free versions of my favorite treats. Maybe we can sell them at the event to raise some money for the food bank. That’s cool! I’ve never made anything like that before, but I’m excited to try. What do you use instead of dairy? Oh, you can use things like almond milk, coconut oil, and oat flour. It’s a bit different, but the results are really good. I’ve been experimenting with it for a while now.

Mm, so, I was thinking about the car accident that happened last week. Did you hear about it? Yeah, I did. It was pretty scary, wasn’t it? A van hit a car on the A25. Was it near here? I think it was on the way to the seaside. The driver was lucky, I guess. But it all happened so fast. I couldn’t believe it. I know, it’s so sad. It makes me think about how dangerous the roads can be. You know, I used to be really scared of driving, but now I’m more relaxed. Although, I still get nervous when the weather’s bad. I’m not a big fan of driving either. I’d rather take the bus or the train. You know, I was thinking about the school play we did last year –  Alice in Wonderland . Do you remember when we had to wear costumes? Oh, how could I forget! I remember you had this huge puffball hat and a dress that was all ruffles. It was so funny, and everyone loved it. You even got a standing ovation. I know, and it wasn’t even that good of a performance. But it was fun. I wonder if we’ll do anything like that again. I’d like to act more, but I’m not sure if I have the confidence. You’ve come a long way since that play, sweetheart. You’ve got a talent for drama. Why don’t you try joining the school theatre group? It could be a great way to meet new people and improve your confidence. Maybe. I’ve been thinking about it, actually. I’ve been reading a lot of plays lately. I like Shakespeare, but I also enjoy modern plays. Have you read  The Lion King  as a play? It’s so dramatic. Oh yes, I love that one. It’s such a powerful story. I think you’d really enjoy it. Speaking of plays, I’ve been thinking about going to the local theatre. There’s a new production of  Macbeth  starting next month. That sounds amazing. I’d love to go with you. But I’m not sure if I go to the theatre much. I’ve always preferred reading or watching movies. It’s okay. You can start with something lighter, like a comedy. The latest  West End  show is really popular.

I just had a call from one of the local protest groups, you know the one that's been fighting against the wind turbines being put up near the village. It's getting really intense, isn't it? Yeah, I heard about it. I think they've been meeting quite a lot, trying to get more support. But I don't think they're really ready for what's coming next. They need a proper strategy, not just shouting and waving placards. Exactly. It's not just about getting angry and stopping the plans. They need to be well-informed. I told them last night that without proper research, they won’t be able to challenge the planning applications properly. You can't just rely on opinion anymore. I know, and I think the council is dragging their feet on the planning appeal too. They’re not taking the community’s concerns seriously enough, are they? They’re more focused on the energy companies and the subsidies they get. That’s the politics of it, isn’t it? The local planners are under pressure from the council and the energy firms. They don’t want to lose out on the money that comes with those projects. But the people who live nearby, like us, aren’t getting a fair shake. And the protesters are up against a system that’s built to support these developments. It’s not just about stopping the turbines; it’s about changing the whole approach to energy. We need better storage solutions, more research, and a better way of generating power that doesn’t harm the environment or the local community. You’re right. The government gives a lot of money to energy companies for subsidies, but not enough to researchers or for developing new, sustainable technologies. That’s a real problem. If we’re going to have clean energy, we need to invest in research that supports that. And we need to make sure that the voices of the local people are heard. I think the Scottish referendum is going to have a big impact on this. If Scotland goes independent, it might change how energy policies are handled. We could see more support for renewable energy in the long run. Yeah, but even if the referendum passes, it’s going to take a while for things to change. The system is set in stone, and it’s going to take a lot of pressure from the public to shift the balance.

Well, I've been meaning to talk to you about the car. I've had a few calls from the insurance company, and they've been asking about the driving test. I think it's time you got your licence, lass. You've been driving the van for a while now, haven't you? Yeah, I’ve been doing it for a few months now, Dad. It’s not like I’ve been hiding from it. I’ve got the theory done, and I’ve been practicing in the driveway. I think I’m ready to take the test. Oh, well, I remember when I first got my licence. It was a bit of a nightmare. I had to take it three times before I finally passed. You’d think with today’s cars and all the automatics, it’d be easier, but no, it’s just as difficult. Well, I can tell you this, lass—don’t take any shortcuts. You drive in the driveway, but you’ll need to handle real roads. You’ll be on the motorway soon, and that’s no place for a nervous driver. I know, Dad. I’ve been thinking about it a lot. I’ve even been checking out the insurance rates. I don’t want to put you out, but I think it’s time I started paying my own way. I’ve got a part-time job now, and I can cover the costs. Oh, you’re getting independent, aren’t you? That’s good. But remember, you’re still family. If you need help, don’t hesitate to ask. I know your gran and I helped you through the first few weeks when you were learning. Yeah, and we’ll be there for you when the time comes. The key thing is to stay calm. You know that highway driving is the hardest part. You’ve got to keep your eyes on the road and not get distracted by anything. I know, Dad. I’ve been told that a million times. I’m just trying to be responsible. I don’t want to rush into it. I want to make sure I’m ready. I’ve got the practical test booked for next week, but I’m not going to take it if I’m not fully prepared. That’s the attitude. I think you’ll do fine. You’ve always been a quick learner.

So, Dad, I just got a message from my mates saying they’re planning a trip to Brighton next month. I was wondering if you’d like to come with us? Brighton? That’s a long way from here, love. I’ve got a bit of a knee problem, and I don’t think I’d be able to manage the walk to the beach. Plus, I’m not sure how I’d get there with all these new regulations about parking these days. Yeah, I know, but it’s just a few days. And you could take the train, or maybe even a car if you like. I could drive you over and pick you up. That sounds nice, but I’m not sure. I haven’t really been out much since the lockdown. I’ve been watching the racing on TV, but it’s not the same as being there. I remember when we used to go to the races in the 50s. It was all in the open air, you know. There was no such thing as WiFi or Facebook, but we had real conversations. Yeah, I know. I’ve been thinking about that too. Like, how do you even remember the days before everything went digital? It’s so different now. It’s not just the technology – it’s the whole way of life. People used to know each other. You knew your neighbour, you knew the shopkeeper, you even knew the people who worked at the post office. Now, you just scroll through apps and get notifications all the time. I can’t even look at my phone without getting a message or an alert. Even when I’m trying to relax, it’s like the world keeps pulling me back in. I know what you mean. I used to be quite good at ignoring it. But now, even the TV is full of ads and social media. It’s like the whole world is constantly screaming at you. I guess that’s one of the downsides of living in this age. But I miss the old ways. I remember my mum used to make the best tea and biscuits. She’d always have a pot on the go. Now, people just reach for a packet of biscuits and a sugary drink. Mm, that’s true. I think it’s got to do with the pace of life.

So, do you remember that time we tried to play Shakespeare at the pub? Oh yeah, that was a disaster. You were doing  Hamlet  and you somehow turned it into a comedy about a guy who owned a kebab shop. Yeah, it was hilarious in hindsight. I think I even got a laugh from the barmaid. She said, “I don’t know what that was, but I’m still buying you a drink.” Classic. You always did have a way of making even the most serious drama sound like a sitcom. But seriously, what’s the deal with Shakespeare? I mean, I get it’s important, but why do people still make jokes about it? I think it’s partly because it’s so over the top. You know, like, how do you even  act  in a play where everyone’s talking in metaphors? I tried once to do  Macbeth  and I accidentally said “I’d rather be a dog” instead of “I’d rather be a king.” Oh man, that’s a real killer line. You really nailed it. I didn’t. I was just trying to sound deep and I messed it up. You’re not the only one. I once tried to do  Romeo and Juliet  and ended up quoting  Friends  instead. That’s not a bad strategy. You’d have a better chance of winning the audience over with a reference to Joey Tribbiani than a bunch of sonnets. Exactly. I think the whole point is to make Shakespeare  accessible . But then again, I did once try to walk into a lecture on the Renaissance and ended up arguing with the professor about what the “true” meaning of  The Tempest  was. That’s not  walking  into a lecture, that’s  charging  into a battle. And I won. He said I had a “sparkling interpretation.” Yeah, and that’s what you get for always trying to sound smarter than you are. Okay, but you remember when we tried to learn golf? I hit the ball straight into a tree. Oh, that was epic. You said, “It’s like I’m trying to play  Minecraft  but with a ball.” Exactly. You were the only one who could make it sound like a game. And you know what’s funny? I still don’t know how to swing a club properly. I think I’ve been trying to “win” at golf, but all I’ve done is make a mess of the course.

So, how’s the new job going, then? I heard you got promoted last month. Oh, yeah, it’s been a bit of a rollercoaster. I had to learn a whole new set of processes, but I’m getting the hang of it. Just wish the hours weren’t so long. I’m exhausted most of the time. I know what you mean. I’m still working the same hours as before, but now I’m managing a team. It’s a lot more pressure. I haven’t had time to go out with friends like I used to. Yeah, I can imagine. I’m still working a lot, but at least I’ve got a bit more freedom in what I do. I’ve been trying to plan a weekend trip to somewhere, maybe the coast? Drove up to Scarborough last week, and it was brilliant. The sun was out, and the beach was packed. That sounds nice. I’ve been meaning to get out more. I’ve been working so much I’ve forgotten how to switch off. I’ve even started eating more junk food—like, I’ve been up to three takeaway meals a week. It’s gotten out of hand, honestly. You can't be serious. I’ve been trying to cut down on my own. I’ve been trying to eat more healthily, but it’s so hard when you’re busy and just want something quick. I’ve been watching a cooking show on BBC, and it's making me think about trying to cook more. Oh, I love that show. It’s so inspiring. I’ve been trying to cook more at home too. I’ve even started a small garden at my flat. I’m growing some herbs and a few veggies. It’s not much, but it’s a start. That sounds amazing. I’ve always wanted to have a garden, but I don’t know where to start. My flat doesn’t even have a balcony. I’ve been thinking about renting a place with a garden, though. I mean, I’m not in a rush, but it’s something to aim for. Yeah, I’ve been looking at places too. I want something a bit more spacious. I’m living with roommates now, but it’s getting a bit crowded. I’m seriously thinking of moving out on my own, even if it’s just a small flat.

Well, I've just been on Skype with my son, and he’s been telling me about this eclipse that's coming up next month. He said it's going to be a total eclipse, and he’s planning to go to somewhere where it's going to be visible. Oh, I heard about that. I thought it was going to be an annular one, but I guess it depends on where you are. I wonder if we'll get to see it here in Norfolk. I think it’s going to be a total eclipse here. Didn’t the sun get blocked out a bit last time? It was like a big shadow over the sky. Yeah, it was strange. It got pretty dark, and I remember the birds stopping singing. It was like night-time, but it wasn’t raining or anything. That must have been scary, especially for someone who doesn’t know what to expect. I’d be nervous if I saw something like that for the first time. Well, I suppose it’s a natural thing, but I still find it a bit spooky. I mean, I don’t like the idea of the sun disappearing like that. I know, it’s a bit unnerving, but it’s also fascinating. My son’s talking about planning a trip and setting up a camera to take pictures. He wants to capture the moment when the sun disappears. That’s a good idea. I suppose you have to be in the right place at the right time. It’s one of those things you can’t just watch on a screen. You have to be there. Yeah, I remember when I was a child, we used to watch the moon and the sun, but now I just take care of the garden and worry about the plants. Speaking of plants, have you seen the bamboo growing near the back? It’s getting taller every day. I think it’s going to take over the whole garden if we don’t do something about it. It’s a bit of a mess, but I like the way it looks. It adds some greenery to the place. I think it’s a good idea to let it grow, as long as it doesn’t get too wild. I think I’ll plant some more flowers around it. I’ve been trying to get the garden to look nice again.

So, do you know where we're going? I mean, I think we said something about going to that new Italian place in Hexham? Or was it somewhere else? No, no, I think we were talking about going to that place in Bishop Auckland. The one with the really good pasta? I saw a review online the other day, and it said the tagliatelle was out of this world. Oh, yeah! That’s the one. I remember seeing it on some food blog. But wait, how are we getting there? Are we taking the bus? I don’t think there’s a direct train from here. No, the train only goes as far as Bishop’s Stortford, and then you have to take a bus. But I think there’s a bus service that goes from there to Bishop Auckland. I might need to check the timetable again before we leave. Yeah, I guess that’s the way to go. But do you know what time the bus leaves? I’m not sure if I want to wait too long. I mean, it’s not like we have a lot of time to kill. It leaves at 8:45, so we need to be there by 8:30. That gives us enough time to grab a coffee or something. Though I think it’s a bit of a drive from here. It’s not like we can just zip over there in a few minutes. Honestly, I’d rather drive. I mean, I don’t like the buses here. I mean, they’re not that bad, but sometimes the buses are delayed and you end up waiting for ages. I’ve had it with being stuck on a bus for an hour just to get somewhere 20 minutes away. I get that. But driving takes longer, and it’s a bit of a long way. Plus, if we drive, we might end up getting lost. I’ve tried to take that route before, and it was a bit of a nightmare. I know, I know. But I think I have a better idea. What if we just plan to go to that place in Hexham instead? I think it’s a bit closer. Plus, I remember there’s a good Italian place on the High Street there. Hexham? Yeah, that could work. But I think the one in Bishop Auckland is better. It’s more central, and I think they’ve got a great selection of wines.

Oh, do you hear that? It’s a wren. I think it’s just outside the window. That’s got to be it. I’ve been trying to identify the birds all week. Oh, I thought it was a sparrow at first, but you’re right—it’s definitely a wren. I’ve been feeding them in the garden all winter. They’ve got such little beaks, but they’re such persistent little things. I know, they’re so cute. I’ve started to get into birdwatching, actually. It’s a bit of a hobby now. You know, like, I’ve even got a little book with all the different birds and their calls. That’s a great idea. I’ve always found birdsong fascinating. I think I’m going to try that. But I’m not sure if the little ones here will even stick around. I mean, we’re still in the middle of winter. Yeah, but the wren’s always around, even in the cold. I think they’re one of the first birds to come out of hibernation. I remember reading somewhere that they can survive quite well in the cold as long as they have something to eat. That’s interesting. I’ve been feeding them seeds and suet – I don’t know if that’s enough, but they seem to like it. I’ve got this old bird feeder up in the tree, and it’s always full by morning. It’s kind of become a ritual now. That’s lovely. It’s amazing how much joy you can get from something so simple. I think I might be getting into that too. I’ve been feeling a bit down lately, and being out in the garden helps. Oh, I’m sorry to hear that. You know, I had a conversation with the dentist yesterday about how important it is to take care of your mental health. He said that if you’re not feeling well, it can start to affect your physical health too. That’s true. I’ve been having some nosebleeds lately, and I think it’s because of the dry air. I’ve been told to use a humidifier, but I haven’t got one. I’m just hoping the weather changes soon. Yeah, the weather’s been so odd this year. One day it’s bright and sunny, the next day it’s pouring with rain.

So, how’s everything going? It’s been a while since we last caught up. How’s the new job treating you? Oh, it’s good, thank you. It’s a bit of a change from what I was doing before, but I think I’m settling in. How about you? Still teaching at that school? Yeah, still there. I’ve actually been thinking about a change. A lot of things have been on my mind lately, especially with the whole IVF thing. You know, I’ve been meaning to talk about it. Oh, I know. I heard you were going through it. How’s it going? Are you still trying? Yeah, it’s been a bit of a rollercoaster. It’s not easy, you know. You feel like you’re doing everything right, but sometimes it just doesn’t work out. And honestly, it’s exhausting—both physically and emotionally. I can only imagine. I’ve been there too, you know. I had to do it once. It was tough, but I pushed through. You know, I ended up having one child through IVF, and it was worth it. It’s just that the journey was… intense. Yeah, I know. It’s not just about the science—it’s about the emotional toll. Sometimes I wonder if I’m ready for it. I’ve got a lot on my plate with my kids already. I’m single, and I’m just starting to think about adding someone else to the mix. I can definitely understand that. Single parenthood is a lot, and then adding another child—well, it’s not something you take lightly. I mean, I was single too when I had my kid. It was scary, but I made it work. That’s true. I admire you for that. I guess I’m just overthinking it. I mean, I’ve been on social media lately, and it’s like everyone’s got their lives together. You know, smiling, happy, everything’s perfect. It’s hard not to feel like I’m falling behind. I know what you mean. Social media can be really misleading. It’s like everyone’s living their best life, but in reality, people are just as stressed and overwhelmed as everyone else. I find that yoga helps me deal with it. It’s a bit of a reset, you know? I’ve heard about yoga.

So, do you know, I’ve been thinking a lot about education lately. It’s such a big deal these days, isn’t it? Especially with all the changes in schools and how they’re trying to prepare kids for the future. I know, it’s been on my mind too. I mean, I was a teacher for thirty years, so I’ve seen it all. From the days when a blackboard was all you needed to the way things are now, with all these gadgets and technology. It’s a different world. Yeah, I can imagine. I’ve been teaching languages for the past ten years, mostly at the secondary level. It’s tough, but I love it. You get to meet so many different people and see how language can really open doors. That sounds good, but I’ve been thinking about how the younger generation is so much more into their own things. I remember when I was teaching, everyone wanted to be in the same class, you know? Now, they’re more into social media and games. I think that’s just the way it is. People change, and so do the times. But I still think it’s important to encourage kids to learn. It’s not just about grades, it’s about building skills that will help them in life. I agree, but I’ve also seen a lot of parents pushing their kids too hard. You know, the pressure to get into the best schools and the best universities. It’s almost like a competition. That’s true. I’ve had students who are under a lot of pressure from their families. It’s hard for them to find a balance between school and their own interests. I remember when my kids were younger. They had their own things they were into, and I let them explore. Now, I see my grandkids and they’re already obsessed with apps and gaming. I wonder what they’ll be doing in ten years. I guess it’s hard to predict. But I do think having hobbies and interests outside of school can be really beneficial. It helps people develop a well-rounded personality. Yeah, I think you’re right. I’ve been trying to get back into some hobbies myself lately. I’ve been thinking about taking up gardening. I’ve always loved plants, but I never had the time.

Alright, so I just got back from the weekend and I had the most amazing meal. We went to this little place in the village, and they served this proper Yorkshire pie. It was like, I don’t know, it hit all the right notes. You know, proper flaky pastry, juicy meat, everything. Oh yeah, I’ve heard about that place. I think it’s called The Butcher’s Arms or something like that. I’ve been meaning to go there for a while. What did you have? I had the lamb. Didn’t even need any gravy, just the meat and the crispy crust. It was so good, I almost cried. I mean, not literally, but I was like, “This is what I’m talking about.” That sounds incredible. I’m not a huge fan of meat, but I do love good food in general. What about you, Liam? What did you do over the weekend? Honestly, I just stayed in. I was catching up on some Netflix and eating a ton of popcorn. I’ve been trying to watch more independent films lately, though. I think I’m going to see  The Power of the Dog  next. It’s been getting a lot of buzz. Oh, I’ve heard about that one. I think it’s a bit heavy, but I’m curious. I’ve been meaning to see more of those kinds of movies. I’m more of a rom-com guy, to be honest. Yeah, I’m not a big fan of heavy dramas either. I do love some good music, though. I’ve been listening to a lot of indie stuff lately. Have you heard of The National? I think they’re from the US, but the music is really atmospheric. I’ve heard of them. I love that kind of sound. I’m more into something like Sigur Rós for the dreamy stuff. But I can appreciate a good indie band too. Speaking of music, did any of you go to any gigs recently? I did actually. There was this small venue in Cambridge, and they had this local band playing. It was really good. I think the lead singer had a really powerful voice. It made me think about how much music can move people. That does happen, doesn’t it? Music is like therapy sometimes. I mean, when I’m stressed out, I just crank up some heavy metal and I feel better.

So, do you think we should go to the gym tomorrow? I’ve been trying to get back into shape after that weekend trip. Honestly, I’m still recovering from the weekend. I mean, we went to that festival, and I didn’t even get a chance to lift a weight. But I guess it’s time to get back on track. Yeah, I’ve been thinking the same thing. I’ve been working out three times a week, but I’m not seeing the results I wanted. Maybe I need to change my routine or add some new exercises. You know, I’ve been thinking about trying a new gym. I heard there’s this place in Cambridge that has some really good equipment and a great vibe. It’s got a bit of a techno vibe, which I actually like. Hmm, techno? You mean like the kind of music they play at the gym? Yeah, exactly. It keeps you motivated. I don’t know, maybe it’s just my thing. I’ve been listening to more electronic music lately, and I think it fits well with the gym environment. I’m more of a classic rock guy. I think the music should match the mood of the workout. Like, if it’s a heavy workout, I like heavy music. If it’s a light jog, maybe something more mellow. I don’t know, I think music’s a personal thing. I’ve heard that some people even use White Noise or just music without lyrics. It helps them focus on their form. That’s interesting. I’ve tried that before, but I found it hard to stay motivated without some kind of beat. Maybe I should give it a try. Speaking of music, I was thinking about a trip to Spain. I know it’s been a while since we went, but I think it’s time for a change of scenery. The weather’s been so gloomy here lately. Spain sounds good. I’ve been wanting to go to Barcelona for a while. I heard the beaches are amazing, and the cities are really vibrant. Plus, the food is amazing. I’ve been thinking about that too. I’ve got this travel blog I started, and I go on a few trips each year to document my experiences. I think next year I’ll go to Croatia. The coast there is stunning.

I can't believe the amount of goals they scored in that match. I mean, it was like they just wanted to win and didn't care about the score at all. Yeah, I know, it was wild. I mean, they had like five or six chances in the first half, and they just didn’t convert any of them. It was ridiculous. I think the ref was actually on their side or something. Honestly, I don’t even know what the point of the game was. If it’s just about scoring, then maybe they should’ve called a timeout or something. But no, they just kept going. I mean, I can’t even remember the last time I saw such a one-sided game. I remember you saying something like that last week when we were talking about the match between Manchester United and Liverpool. You said the same thing—like, it was a complete disaster. And here we are again, with this happened. Maybe the teams are just not competing properly. I don’t know. Maybe the players are just overthinking it. I mean, it’s football—there’s supposed to be some tension, some excitement. But this was like watching a bunch of robots play. No passion, no intensity. It was just... flat. I know, it’s been a bit of a downer these days. I mean, the Premier League is supposed to be the best in the world, right? But lately, it feels like it’s just a bunch of players going through the motions. I wonder if it's the pressure of the game or the way the media is constantly talking about the players’ personal lives. Maybe it's also the Easter break. I mean, people are away on holidays, the teams aren’t resting properly, and they’re just not in the right mindset. I know I’ve been feeling it too. Maybe I need to take a break from watching football for a while. I can’t take it anymore. Yeah, I was thinking the same thing. I tried to watch a few games last week, but I just couldn’t get into it. It’s like the excitement has gone. I wonder what’s going to happen when the season gets back on track. I mean, I still go to games on weekends, if you know what I mean. But lately, even the atmosphere is just not the same.

So, do you remember when we first brought the boys home from the hospital? It was like the whole world changed in an instant. I remember everything about that day, actually. You were so tired, but you still managed to smile the whole time. Yeah, and it was such a strange feeling, having them both in the same room. I kept checking to make sure they were both breathing. Oh, I remember that. You were so nervous, Eileen. I think you even cried when the nurse said they were both doing well. I was just so relieved. I mean, bringing two kids into the world is a big deal, especially when you're still figuring out your life. It was overwhelming at first, but then things started to settle. We had to learn how to take care of them, how to feed them, how to make sure they slept. I remember when they started going to the park. You used to take them every weekend, even when it was raining. It was like you could never get enough of them. You did your best, Eileen. And you did it with such love. I remember watching you with them – it was like you were glowing. I guess I was, in a way. It was the best feeling in the world. But there were moments when I felt like I wasn’t doing enough. You were doing more than enough. You were giving them a home, a family, and a love that they’ll never forget. I still look at the photos from when they were babies, and it feels like yesterday. I can’t believe they’re already talking and running around like little tornadoes. Oh, they’ll be big ones soon. I remember when they started asking about their birthdays. You used to plan the whole thing – cake, presents, and even a special movie. I wanted them to have the best childhoods possible. Even if it meant working late and missing some of their milestones. And you did. I think they’re growing up with such a strong sense of family. They always ask about their grandparents, about the stories we tell them about their parents. I just hope they remember all of this. That they know how much love and effort went into raising them. They will. They always do. Even now, when they come over to visit, they talk about the holidays, the trips we took, and even the time we went to the cinema.

So, do you remember when we were kids and we used to play that game with the wooden blocks? The one where you had to build a house and then knock it down? I think it was called ‘It’s a Small World’ or something like that. Oh yes, I remember that. We used to use the old blocks from the shed, and we’d build these elaborate castles. My brother used to be the king, and I was the princess. I think we even had a tiny bed for the prince made out of cardboard. Oh, I remember that too. I think you used to have to build it in a certain way so it wouldn’t fall down. I still remember how stressed you got when it collapsed after ten minutes. Oh, you were always so meticulous. I think you even made a little flag out of the old newspaper to put on top of the castle. It was a tiny little thing, but you were proud of it. Yes, and then we’d have to knock it down and rebuild it again. It was like a competition. I think we even had a rule that you had to use all the blocks each time. It was quite strict, actually. I remember watching you two argue over where to put the blocks. It was so funny. You were always so competitive, and I was just the one who helped you carry the blocks. I used to feel like the assistant in the game. And we used to play this other game with the knitting needles. I think my mum used to teach us how to do the simplest things, like making a scarf or a small cushion. I still remember the smell of the wool and how it felt in your hands. Yes, the wool was different then. It wasn’t as synthetic as it is now. I think you used to get it from the local shop in Peterborough. It was always warm and soft, and it smelled like home. Oh, and then there was the ‘It’s a Small World’ song. We used to sing it while we played. I think that was the one time we all sang together. It was like a little ritual. I think you remember when we got this old TV that played the ‘It’s a Small World’ song from the Disney film.

Well, I've just had a cup of tea and a sandwich. It's nice and warm, isn't it? Yes, it’s a good day, isn’t it? A bit chilly, though. I think the sun’s coming out again later. I hope so. I’d like to go out for a walk, but I reckon it’ll be too cold. Though I’ve been meaning to take a stroll down by the river. That’d be lovely. The river’s been looking rather nice lately, especially after the rain. The ducks are all out on the water, flapping around like they always do. Aye, they’re a bit of a nuisance, really. I’ve seen one land on the grass and just sit there, looking at me like it’s got a mind of its own. Oh, you’re always saying that. I think they’re just trying to get some food. You know, they’re not actually naughty, are they? No, I suppose not. They just do what they have to. I’ve always thought they’re clever, though. I’ve seen them move things around, like they’re trying to build a little nest or something. Hmm, maybe they are. I’ve heard that some ducks actually build nests in the reeds. I think it’s the mallards, the ones with the yellow feet. Yeah, I suppose they are. I always get a bit excited when I see a family of them out there. They’re so graceful, aren’t they? They are. I remember when I was a girl, we used to go to the countryside all the time. I think my dad used to take us out on the river in a little boat. That sounds nice. I never had that, though. I was always too busy working. Well, you worked hard. I think it’s nice to have a bit of time now, even if it’s just sitting here having a chat. Aye, it’s a good thing. I’ve got the time, and I think I’ll take it. I’ve been feeling a bit more sprightly lately, haven’t I? You have. You’ve been making me laugh more than usual, too. You’ve got your jokes still, even at your age. Oh, I think it’s the tea. You can’t deny it. Yeah, maybe. Or maybe it’s just that we’re both getting a bit older and we’ve got more time to sit and chat.

So how’s life treating you, Jess? You’ve been quiet since we last met. Oh, I’ve been good, thanks. Just been swamped with work. You know how it is, teaching can be really demanding. Yeah, I can totally relate. I’m a copywriter now, and it’s a different kind of pressure. You have to be on top of your game all the time. I hear you. But I think being a teacher is like being a parent in a way. You’re always looking out for your students. That’s true. I feel like I’ve become a bit of a mentor to some of them. It’s not just about teaching, it’s about shaping their future. That’s beautiful, but I feel like I’ve been more of a ‘content creator’ lately. Writing ads for companies, trying to sell whatever they need. It’s not as personal. I can imagine that being a bit draining. Have you ever thought about moving into something more… creative? Honestly, I’ve thought about it a lot. But I’ve got a few clients who’ve been with me for years, so it’s hard to break away. Plus, I love the challenge of coming up with new ideas. That’s admirable. I’m actually thinking of doing a masters in education. I’ve been feeling like I need more training, especially with the new curriculum. That sounds like a great move. I remember when I started teaching, I had no idea what I was getting into. Yeah, I can only imagine. I have about five friends who are teachers, and they all talk about it like it’s the hardest job in the world. It is, but it’s also one of the most rewarding. You get to make a real difference in someone’s life. Absolutely. I think that’s why I love it. I’ve had some really memorable moments with my students. There was one who used to come in every day with a smile, and now he’s applying to university. That’s amazing. I’ve had a few pets over the years, but I think I’m going to start a cat or something soon. I just need to find the right one. A cat would be perfect. I’ve had a dog for years, and it’s been one of the best decisions I’ve ever made.

So, do you live in the same area as your family, or have you moved out? Well, I live with my mum and dad, actually. We’ve been together since I was a kid. It’s not the best place, but it’s home. Yeah, I understand. I grew up in a similar place, but I moved out years ago. It’s a bit of a toss-up, but I think being close to family has its perks. Honestly, I haven’t even thought about moving out. I mean, I don’t even know what I’d do. My flatmates are like family, I guess. Yeah, I think about that sometimes. I mean, I’m still at school, but I’ve been thinking about what I want to do after. Maybe I’ll live with my cousin or something. That’s a good idea. You know, living with family or friends can be a great way to start. Just don’t get stuck in the wrong place. It’s not just about the place, though. It’s about the people you’re with. I mean, I live with my parents, but I’m not always happy with how things are run around here. Yeah, I can see that. I mean, sometimes it feels like there’s not enough space, or the place is just too small. I’ve heard that about a lot of places in Liverpool. It’s a great city, but the housing is a bit of a nightmare. I know. I mean, I’ve seen some of the places people live in, and it’s not even close to what I’d call safe. I agree. I think the lack of housing is a bigger issue than people think. People are forced to live in places that aren’t safe for their families. And it’s not just about safety. It’s about stability. If you can’t get a proper place, it’s hard to get a proper job, and then that affects everything else. Yeah, I’ve heard people talk about that. I mean, I’m not even in a stable job yet, but I can see how it would make life harder. Exactly. I think the government needs to do more about it, but until then, people are just trying to make the best of what they’ve got. I wonder if anyone even cares.

I've been thinking a lot about our trip to Nepal, you know. I was just reading about it in  The Guardian  and it really struck me how beautiful the places are, especially the mountains. It’s a shame we haven’t planned it yet. Yes, I agree. I’ve always wanted to go there, especially after the one I did to Morocco years ago. I still remember that spice market in Marrakesh – it was like stepping back in time. But Nepal? I’ve heard it’s even more remote and magical. Didn’t you go to the Festival of Lights in Jaipur, Helen? I think it was a few years back. You told us about how the whole city lit up like a dream. Oh yes, that was incredible. We had to walk through the streets, and the lights reflected off the water in the tanks, it was like something out of a picture book. But I do miss the local food – the street food was amazing. I remember you saying the lentil curry was like a revelation. I’ve been trying to recreate it ever since, but I can never get the taste quite right. Haha, I tried once, and it tasted more like a stew than a curry. You really have to use the right spices, I think. But I suppose that’s part of the adventure, isn’t it? Definitely. Speaking of adventures, have you seen the Tour of Britain lately? It passed through our area last week, and it was a madhouse. I had to queue for hours just to get a photo. Oh yes, I remember that. My daughter was training for an Iron Man event and she was so excited to see the cyclists. I think she said it made her feel like she was part of something bigger. That’s lovely. My son’s got into triathlons too, though he’s more into the swimming part than the running. He mentioned he’s planning to do a half Iron Man next year. I hope he doesn’t overdo it. He’s got a good head on his shoulders, though. I think he’s got the same determination as my husband did when he started his own business. Though he didn’t do triathlons, he did have to manage a lot of things at once. You know what’s funny is that when I was younger, I used to think that’s what I wanted – to be running my own business.

So, do you ever find it weird how we’re all in such similar jobs but still manage to be so different? Like, I mean, I’m a conference and events co-ordinator, you’re a production controller, and Lucy’s an admin secretary. But we all seem to be stuck in the same kind of bracket, don’t you think? Honestly, yeah, it’s kind of weird. I mean, we’re all in the same age range too, but we’ve got such different paths. I know you’re the one who’s always been the planner, you know? Like, the one who’s got all the event details memorized, and everything is always running smoothly because of you. Oh, please. I still get lost in my own head half the time. I mean, I had to Google what a “production controller” even meant the other day. It’s like, how do you even describe that job to someone who doesn’t understand it? Honestly, I think it’s a bit of a mystery to everyone. I mean, I’m just an admin assistant, and even I don’t know what I’m supposed to be doing half the time. It’s like, I’m in a job that sounds important, but I’m just typing things into a spreadsheet all day. Mate, you’re the one with the postgrad degree. Shouldn’t you be doing something more…  exciting ? Oh, don’t get me wrong, I love what I do. It’s just that I think my dream was to work in publishing or something. But then I got this job, and I’m like… “Okay, I’ll make do.” You know? It’s about stability, right? Yeah, but I feel like we’re all just doing things that aren’t quite what we wanted. I mean, I’m in events, and I love that, but I keep thinking, “What if I had gone into marketing?” or “What if I had started my own business instead of working for someone else?” I get that. I was always the type of person who wanted to start their own business. I mean, I’ve got all the skills, and I’m good with people. But every time I try to talk about it, my parents are like, “You’re so young, you don’t know what you’re talking about.” You know what’s funny?

So, do you know what’s going on with the library? I’ve been trying to get some information about the petition, but it’s all so muddled up. Yeah, I saw a poster outside the café the other day. They’re planning to demolish it and build a new shopping centre in its place. It’s shocking, really. I mean, the library’s been there for years. I know, and I think that’s why we need to start a petition. It’s not just about the books; it’s about the community. We’ve got so many kids who use it for study space, and it’s a vital resource. Absolutely. I’ve been thinking about it too. My mum used to take me there when I was a kid. I can’t imagine not having that place anymore. But how do we even start? We need signatures, right? That’s the thing—maybe we can go to the local council meeting next week. I heard they’re discussing the planning application. If we can get a few people to sign up, we might stand a chance. Yeah, but I don’t think the council is going to listen to us. They’ve been pushing for this development for ages. I remember reading in the paper that they’re negotiating with a big estate developer. That’s really worrying. But we can’t just sit back and do nothing. I mean, even if it’s a long shot, we should try. Our kids, our families, our whole community rely on that library. I agree. I’m just worried about the work shifts though. I’ve got a shift tomorrow, and I can’t really make it to the meeting. I’m not sure I can manage without the library either. I can help you with that. I know some people who have the same kind of shift pattern. Maybe we can coordinate. It’s worth trying. Thanks. I’ll message them and see if they can make it. Oh, and I saw you on your phone earlier—what were you doing? Oh, just trying to remember some mnemonics for work. My boss keeps telling me I need to remember more details for the transcriptions. I’ve been doing some brain training on my app, but it’s not helping much. That’s funny. I’ve been doing the same thing.

So, do you know what’s up with the Jehovah’s Witnesses around here? They’ve been knocking on doors like it’s the end of the world again. I swear, I’ve seen more of them in the past week than in the whole of last year. Oh, they’re just trying to spread the word, I suppose. I’ve got one neighbor who’s totally converted. He used to be a regular sceptic, but now he’s got that look in his eye like he’s seen the truth. Yeah, and it’s not like they’re being pushy or anything. I mean, they just sit on your doorstep and talk. I don’t mind them, honestly, but I do wonder what they think about our village. I mean, who’s gonna believe all that stuff about the world ending? I’d say not many. But then again, I’m not a religious man. Wait, does anyone know if any of the kids here are getting married soon? I heard there’s a couple from the village planning something for the summer. Oh, I think I heard something about that. There’s a girl from the village and a guy who works in London.
